abstract.en: The Rav opens by speaking of the special worth of a sefer that a tzaddik learned from, as opposed to the Sefer Chassidim's warning about a sefer from which a wicked person learned. He then turns to a custom among ovdei Hashem to say Tikunei Zohar from Rosh Chodesh Elul until Yom Kippur; he stresses that no one is obligated, and notes that the printers divided the sefer into a portion for each of the forty days. The Tikunei Zohar, he explains, is seventy expositions on the word Bereishis, and it is a preparation for Rosh Hashanah. Through it Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai rectifies Jewish souls in these days, and since all Jews are bound to one another, those who say it help everyone. He closes with the wish that all merit to be rectified and to return to Bereishis, binding themselves to the Ribono shel Olam, and says that one must constantly strengthen oneself in these great days and not let them pass empty.

en: There is a custom among ovdei Hashem to say Tikunei Zohar from Rosh Chodesh Elul until Yom Kippur, though the Rav stresses that no one is obligated.
The printers divided the Tikunei Zohar into a portion for each of the forty days.
The Tikunei Zohar is seventy expositions on the word Bereishis and serves as a preparation for Rosh Hashanah.
Through the Tikunei Zohar, Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai rectifies Jewish souls in these days.
The Rav says one must constantly strengthen oneself in these great days and not let them pass with nothing.

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains that the Aseres Yemei Teshuvah, the Beis HaMikdash and Adam HaRishon are each the hidden point of origin of time, place and soul, which is why each must be searched for, and why these days call for searching and for creating oneself anew.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with the Gemara reading 'Dirshu Hashem b'himatzo' as the ten days from Rosh Hashanah to Yom Kippur, and links them to the other thing the Torah says must be searched for, the place of the Beis HaMikdash, which David HaMelech sought without sleep. He explains that the Mikdash is the Even Shesiyah, the point from which the world grew, and that Har, mountain, relates to herayon, conception, while hirhur, thought, is the 'mountain on top of the mountain'. Using the Sefer Yetzirah's triad of olam, shanah and nefesh, he shows that the Mikdash, Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur, and Adam HaRishon are the origin points of place, time and soul. An origin is elusive, as Shmuel's search for David, the search for the Mikdash's site and the Levi'im's mistake about Rosh Hashanah show. The Sanhedrin's authority, too, comes from the place where Torah, the blueprint of the world, goes forth. He closes that in these days one creates oneself through the shofar and the pesukim, must not sleep, and must search, as the last generation will search for Hashem.

en: The Rav links two things the Torah says must be searched for: Hashem in the ten days of teshuvah, and the site of the Beis HaMikdash.
The Beis HaMikdash is the Even Shesiyah, the point from which Hashem began forming the world, and so it is called a Har, related to herayon, conception.

Following the Sefer Yetzirah, the world exists as olam, shanah and nefesh, and each has a Kodesh HaKodashim and a point of origin: the Mikdash in place, Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur in time, and Adam HaRishon in soul.
Rosh Hashanah is herayon, the conception of the year, while Yom Kippur is hirhur, the thought that precedes it, 'the mountain on top of the mountain'.
Every point of origin is elusive and needs searching, because it begins in thought and is not yet tangible.
In the Aseres Yemei Teshuvah one creates oneself anew, through the shofar and the ten pesukim of Malchiyos, Zichronos and Shofros, which correspond to the ten utterances of creation.

title.en: Two things that must be searched for

summary.en: The Rav opens with the Gemara that reads 'Dirshu Hashem b'himatzo' as the ten days from Rosh Hashanah to Yom Kippur, when Hashem is especially accessible. He links this to the Beis HaMikdash, whose site the Torah left for Yidden to search out, as David HaMelech swore not to sleep until he found it.

title.en: The Mikdash as the world's point of origin

summary.en: The Rav explains the Gemara that the Mikdash is 'higher' than Eretz Yisrael: not physically, but as the point on the globe where creation began, the Even Shesiyah and the center of habitation. He explains Har as herayon, conception, and adds that thought, hirhur, comes even before it, like an architect's plan before the building.

title.en: Olam, shanah, nefesh and the forty days

summary.en: Bringing the Sefer Yetzirah's triad of olam, shanah and nefesh, the Rav shows that each has a Kodesh HaKodashim, joined when the Kohen Gadol enters the Kodesh HaKodashim on Yom Kippur. He compares the forty days of an embryo's formation to the forty days from Rosh Chodesh Elul to Yom Kippur, and says that climbing the 'Har Hashem' of Rosh Hashanah requires preparation from Rosh Chodesh Elul.

title.en: Rosh Hashanah, Yom Kippur and Adam HaRishon

summary.en: The Rav shows that Rosh Hashanah is in time what Yerushalayim is in place, the gate of heaven where tefillos rise, and that the Even Shesiyah contains the whole world as Rosh Hashanah contains the whole year. Yom Kippur is hirhur, beyond herayon, and Adam HaRishon, the origin of all mankind, was formed from the place of the Mikdash, uniting the three origins.

title.en: Why the origin is elusive

summary.en: The Rav explains that David HaMelech carries the neshamah of Adam HaRishon and of Mashiach, and that an origin is hard to find because it begins in thought. He shows this from Shmuel, who did not recognize David among Yishai's sons; from David and Shmuel, who first chose the wrong site for the Mikdash; and from the Gemara's story of the Levi'im who erred about whether it was Rosh Hashanah.

title.en: Torah goes forth from Tziyon

summary.en: The Rav brings the zaken mamre, who is liable only when the Sanhedrin sits in the place of the Mikdash, because Torah goes forth from Tziyon. Torah is the blueprint of the world, as he illustrates with the Chazon Ish guiding surgeons from the Torah, so Yerushalayim, the center of the world, should be found in the middle of the Torah, and he looks for it in the middle of Sefer Devarim.

title.en: Creating oneself; not sleeping

summary.en: The Rav explains that in the ten days of teshuvah Hashem tells Yidden to create the world and themselves: through the shofar a new neshamah is blown in, and the ten pesukim of each of Malchiyos, Zichronos and Shofros correspond to the ten utterances of creation. He calls for searching Hashem, the Mikdash and Mashiach, and, like David who was up at night, for not sleeping, bringing the Yerushalmi, Rashi on Yaakov's sleep and the Rambam on the shofar.

title.en: The generation of searchers

summary.en: The Rav says that reaching the peak is not automatic: one can tear off calendar pages and arrive at Rosh Hashanah still at the bottom of the mountain. He speaks of the last generation, 'zeh dor dorshav', who will search for and find Hashem and crown Him, and closes with a call for teshuvah and tzedakah for poor children's Torah learning and with brachos.

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains that in the generation before Moshiach, when the Satan pours out new temptations, small acts of emunah and self-guarding are precious in Heaven, and the greatest danger is the 'kiss' of the nations' culture.

abstract.en: The Rav opens by saying that ours is the generation of the footsteps of Moshiach, when the trials are so hard that small deeds, like holding back a joke or not looking where one should not, give Hashem more pleasure than the great self-sacrifice of earlier generations; he illustrates this with the Ba'al Shem Tov's parable of the king and the talking parrot. He then teaches that the one mitzvah that carries everything is emunah, through a story of souls who demanded to know their purpose, and explains that emunah means never saying 'if only' (volt), since everything is hashgachah pratis. David's silence before Shimi's curse made him the fourth leg of the Divine chariot, because Shimi became the ancestor of Mordechai and Esther, and Purim defeats Amalek, which equals 'doubt'. The Satan, sensing his end, creates new temptations such as television, the internet and cell phones, as the Kohen Gadol needed a miracle on Yom Kippur. Esav's kiss teaches that today the nations bite with friendliness, so bachurim must distance themselves from goyish culture, sports and foods.

en: In the generation before Moshiach the trials are so great that small acts of restraint are worth more in Heaven than the great deeds of earlier generations.
The one mitzvah on which everything stands is emunah, and true emunah means not saying 'if only' about what happened.
Everything, including when and how much a person earns, comes through hashgachah pratis, Divine providence over each detail.
Before Moshiach the Satan is in an emergency, so he creates ever new temptations, and the yetzer hara of today is many times stronger.
Today the nations 'bite with a kiss': their friendliness draws Jews into their culture, and this requires a far greater guarding than in earlier generations.

title.en: Small deeds in the last generation

summary.en: The Rav says this is the generation of the footsteps of Moshiach, when the trials are so hard that small deeds, like holding back a joke at lunch or not looking in the street, outweigh the great deeds of earlier generations. He brings the Ba'al Shem Tov's parable of the king who listened to a talking parrot rather than to his wise men.

title.en: The souls' demand and the mitzvah of emunah

summary.en: The Rav cites the Gemara that Chabakuk based all the mitzvos on one, 'the tzaddik lives by his emunah', and tells a story from a disciple of the Ba'al Shem Tov: souls sent down again and again went from angel to angel demanding their purpose, until they were told that keeping the one mitzvah of emunah would spare them returning. Emunah, he adds, means truly believing and not saying 'volt'.

title.en: What 'volt' means: the late breakfast

summary.en: The Rav explains 'volt' with a parable of a man who missed a lucrative business appointment because there was no milk for breakfast and blamed his wife. The real failure is the 'if only', since everything, how much and when a person earns, is hashgachah pratis from Heaven.

title.en: David, Shimi and the fourth leg of the chariot

summary.en: The Rav tells how Shimi ben Gera cursed David as he fled from Avshalom, and David stopped Avishai from killing him, saying Hashem had told him to curse. At that moment it was decided in Heaven that David would become the fourth leg of the Divine chariot, with Avraham, Yitzchak and Yaakov, and the Rav asks why this act earned it.

title.en: Shimi, Purim and Amalek as doubt

summary.en: The Rav answers that Shimi was the ancestor of Mordechai and Esther, so by sparing him David merited Purim, the defeat of Amalek that completes Hashem's Name and throne. Amalek equals 'safek', doubt, the opposite of emunah, and David's faith that someone else would have cursed him anyway is what made him a leg of the throne.

title.en: The Satan's emergency and the new temptations

summary.en: The Rav explains that for thousands of years the natural yetzer hara from the sin of the Etz HaDaas sufficed, but before Moshiach the Satan has created television, the internet and cell phones. Like a wrestler who is losing, a woman who carried her piano out of a fire, a dying man or a candle that flares before going out, the Satan, knowing he will be slaughtered when Moshiach comes, summons new strength.

title.en: Why the Kohen Gadol needed a miracle

summary.en: The Rav brings the Mishnah in Pirkei Avos that the Kohen Gadol never became impure on Yom Kippur, and the Tosfos Yom Tov's question why this needed a miracle after he stayed awake all night without eating. The answer is that all of Klal Yisroel's atonement depends on him, so the Satan concentrates on him; so too the Satan concentrates on our generation, which needs a far greater guarding.

title.en: Esav's kiss: biting with friendliness

summary.en: The Rav brings Rashi that Esav wanted to bite Yaakov but his neck became like marble, and asks why Esav then kissed him; the answer is that when he could not bite with a bite, he bit with a kiss. For hundreds of years the nations kept Jews in ghettos, but now they are friendly, and that friendliness, through their culture, internet and cell phones, is the bite of the kiss.

title.en: Distance from goyish culture, sports and food

summary.en: The Rav describes how the friendliness of recent popes and of the nations leads to intermarriage, and says one must distance oneself from everything goyish: following ball teams, eating pizza, eating turkey on Thanksgiving. Jews have their own foods for Shabbos and Yom Tov, and he closes that the responsibility to bring Moshiach rests on the bachurim of this generation.

oneLiner.en: Learning the opening of Tanya chapter two with bachurim, the Rav explains how the Jewish soul, 'truly a part of G-d above', stays pure in its innermost point and comes from Hashem's own thought, which no created mind can grasp.

abstract.en: The Rav reviews Tanya chapter one: a Jew has an animal soul from kelipas nogah, which can be elevated when he eats for the sake of Heaven, and a G-dly soul, the subject of chapter two, 'truly a part of G-d above'. He shows this inner point through the Rambam's explanation of why a man forced to say 'I want' brings a valid korban, and through the Ramban's reason for forty lashes: the forty days of a child's formation, of which the first point never sinned, so only thirty-nine are given. The same point appears in the forty days from Rosh Chodesh Elul to Yom Kippur. He explains 'vayipach' as blowing from one's innermost depth, tied to the shofar, and the soul as coming from Hashem's thought and wisdom. Through the mashal of a watch and its maker, and of the five senses, he shows that a creation cannot understand its Creator. He closes with the Tanya's question of why souls differ in level, leaving the answer for next time.

en: The animal soul of a Jew comes from kelipas nogah, so permitted things done for the sake of Heaven are turned to holiness, unlike the three impure kelipos.
According to the Rambam, every Jew has a spark of holiness that truly wants Hashem's will; beating only weakens the evil inclination, so his 'I want' is true.
The Ramban ties forty lashes to the forty days of a child's formation; since the first point of the soul never agreed to the sin, only thirty-nine are given.
'Vayipach', blowing, means bringing out breath from one's innermost being, which shows that the soul comes from Hashem's inner self.
The souls of Jews come from Hashem's thought and wisdom, which is one with Him and cannot be understood by any created mind.
A creation cannot understand its Creator, just as a watch cannot understand its maker, not for lack of intelligence but because it is a different realm entirely.

title.en: Two souls and kelipas nogah

summary.en: The Rav reviews Tanya chapter one: the animal soul of a Jew comes from kelipas nogah, so kosher food eaten for the sake of Heaven is elevated, while the three impure kelipos cannot be. He then opens chapter two, the G-dly soul, 'truly a part of G-d above'.

title.en: The Rambam on 'rotzeh ani'

summary.en: The Rav brings the halachah that one who refuses to bring his korban is beaten until he says 'I want', and the Rambam's answer: every Jew's good inclination truly wants, and the beating only weakens the evil inclination. He then introduces the Torah's forty lashes, of which only thirty-nine are given.

title.en: Forty days of formation and the untouched point

summary.en: The Rav brings the Ramban that forty lashes correspond to the forty days of a child's formation, and explains why only thirty-nine are given: the first point, the G-dly soul, never sinned. He finds the same in the forty days from Rosh Chodesh Elul to Yom Kippur, the day of that point.

title.en: Vayipach: blowing from within

summary.en: The Rav reads the Tanya's proof from 'vayipach be'apav nishmas chayim' and contrasts blowing with speaking: blowing comes with force from one's innermost self. He connects it to Rosh Hashanah and the shofar, to 've'atah nefachtah bi' in the morning blessing, and to the Zohar that one who blows, blows from within.

title.en: Souls from Hashem's thought and wisdom

summary.en: The Rav explains that the world was created for the sake of man, who arose first in Hashem's thought, and that like a child drawn from the father's mind, Jewish souls are drawn from Hashem's wisdom. With the Rambam that Hashem and His wisdom are one, and the mashal of a watch and its maker, he shows why this is beyond understanding.

title.en: Not like our thoughts: the picture and the niggun

summary.en: From 'ki lo machshevosai machshevoseichem' the Rav argues that more intelligence would not help a creation understand its Creator. He gives the mashal of a man who says he heard a beautiful picture or saw a niggun: each thing is grasped only by its own faculty.

title.en: Five senses and the bat

summary.en: The Rav points out that our whole contact with the world comes through five senses, a small number, and that some creatures, like the bat that senses its surroundings by sound in a dark cave, have senses we lack. Even with a million senses, he says, a person would not understand Hashem, because he is the watch and Hashem is the watchmaker.

title.en: Back to the Tanya: why do souls differ?

summary.en: Returning to the Tanya, the Rav reads the Rambam that Hashem is the knower and the known, beyond human grasp, and repeats that Jews come from the 'mind of the Father'. He then raises the Tanya's question: if all souls come from Hashem's thought and Hashem is One, why are there souls of the Avos and Moshe Rabbeinu and souls of the lowest generations? He leaves the answer for the next shiur.

catalogTitle: Chanukah Mashiach ben Yosef and ben David

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains that the Chanukah light is the hidden light of Mashiach, which reaches even the most distant Jewish souls, and shows how Mashiach ben Yosef and Mashiach ben David came into the world through people whose greatness was concealed.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with the Me'or Einayim on the Gemara that wicks and oils unfit for Shabbos may be used for Chanukah, and with the Rokeach, brought by the Bnei Yissaschar, that the hidden light of creation is revealed on Chanukah. Hashem's candles are the souls of Jews. Shabbos lights stay above ten tefachim, but the Chanukah light is lit in the public domain, below ten tefachim, on the left side, at the dark end of the month, to rekindle souls lost in the domain of the Sitra Achra. Every Jew has a hidden love for Hashem that Chanukah brings out. He then finds the light of Mashiach in Vayeshev and Miketz: Yosef and Yehuda, Tamar, Osnas, Dina and even Shechem carried a hidden spark of Mashiach that no one recognized. He closes that just as Yosef suddenly revealed himself to his brothers, a moment will come when the light of Mashiach answers every question.

en: According to the Rokeach, the hidden light of creation is revealed on Chanukah, each person according to his level, and it is the light of Mashiach.
The Rav explains that Hashem's candles are the souls of Jews, and the Chanukah light is lit below ten tefachim in the public domain to rekindle souls that are in the domain of the Sitra Achra.
Wicks too weak for Shabbos burn on Chanukah: souls too far for Shabbos to reach can still be awakened by Chanukah.
Every Jew has a hidden love for Hashem, a spark that can never be extinguished, and Chanukah is a time that brings it out.
Mashiach ben Yosef and Mashiach ben David both come through hidden lights: Yosef, Yehuda, Tamar, Osnas and Dina, whose true greatness was not recognized.
Just as the brothers suddenly understood Yosef when he said 'I am Yosef', a moment will come when the light of Mashiach is revealed and all questions on Hashem's ways are answered.

title.en: Wicks for Chanukah and the hidden light

summary.en: After thanking his hosts, the Rav brings the Me'or Einayim on the Gemara that wicks and oils unfit for Shabbos may be lit on Chanukah, and the Rokeach that the hidden light of creation is revealed on Chanukah. He adds that Hashem too has candles: the souls of Jews, whose brightness is concealed.

title.en: Below ten tefachim in the public domain

summary.en: The Rav explains the public domain as the domain of the Sitra Achra, and brings the Gemara that the Shechinah never descended below ten tefachim, except on Chanukah, whose light is lit at the door, below ten tefachim and on the left side. These lights are Jewish souls who do not properly accept the yoke of Heaven and must be rekindled.

title.en: Light at the dark end of the month

summary.en: Unlike the other Yomim Tovim, which come with a full or growing moon, Chanukah comes at the end of the month in the longest nights. The Rav notes that even Jews who do not keep Shabbos light Chanukah candles, and explains that our kindling below arouses Hashem, like a shadow, to kindle these souls with the light of Mashiach and bring them to teshuvah.

title.en: Eight strings and the hidden love

summary.en: The Rav brings the Gemara that the harp in the Beis HaMikdash had seven strings and that of Mashiach will have eight, so Chanukah's eight days are the light of Mashiach. Every Jew has a hidden love for Hashem that Chanukah brings out, and he returns to the Me'or Einayim: wicks Shabbos cannot ignite, Chanukah can.

title.en: Two Mashiachs in Vayeshev and Miketz

summary.en: The Rav brings the Midrash at the start of Vayeshev that while everyone was busy with his own concerns, the light of Mashiach was being created, and the Gemara and Zohar on the two Mashiachs, ben Yosef and ben David. Yosef was a hidden light his brothers did not recognize, and there was also a time they did not recognize who Yehuda was.

title.en: Yehuda, Tamar and Osnas

summary.en: Yehuda, once leader of the Shevatim, went down from his brothers; both he and Yosef descended below their level to bring Mashiach. Tamar carried the spark of Mashiach ben David and was taken for a zonah, and the Rav tells from the Targum Yonasan and the Midrash how Osnas, daughter of Dina and Shechem, reached Egypt and carried the spark of Mashiach ben Yosef.

title.en: The 'tyrant' and the diamond in Shechem

summary.en: The brothers saw Yosef as a tyrant until he said 'I am Yosef'. The Rav then explains that Shechem himself held a spark of Mashiach ben Yosef, hidden in him like a diamond hidden in a garbage can, and that what befell Dina was planned from Above so this spark could unite with hers.

title.en: Dina's name and Tamar's self-sacrifice

summary.en: The Rav shows that Dina was born with the spark of Mashiach, hinted in her name: spelled out with the full letter names, Dina equals the gematria of Mashiach ben Yosef. He returns to Yehuda's going down and to Tamar, a tzaddekes who risked her life to bring Mashiach and was so concealed that she appeared as a zonah.

title.en: The moment when everything is revealed

summary.en: In one moment Yosef stopped being the tyrant and Tamar was revealed as more righteous than Yehuda. The Rav closes that Jews today ask why they suffer and why Hashem is silent, but a moment will come, like 'I am Yosef', when the light of Mashiach, the light of Chanukah, will be revealed and answer every question.

oneLiner.en: On the yahrtzeit of Rabbi Tzadok HaKohen, the Rav brings his teaching that a Jew shows where he belongs when, in a time of danger, he flees to the Ribono shel Olam.

abstract.en: At a l'chaim on the yahrtzeit of Rabbi Tzadok HaKohen, whose sefarim, the Rav says, we learn as his talmidim, he says that one should say Tachanun in these days even on a yahrtzeit, because the Jewish people need a great yeshuah. Hashem has shown miracles, but one must still ask for rachamim. He then brings a teaching of Rabbi Tzadok on a Mishnah about a creature whose status is in doubt, whether it belongs to the land or to the sea: when it is chased it flees to dry land, and that is the sign that it belongs to the land. From this Rabbi Tzadok learns that in a time of danger a Jew flees to the Ribono shel Olam, and that shows where he belongs.

en: The Rav says one should say Tachanun in these days even on a yahrtzeit, because the Jewish people need a great yeshuah.
Hashem has shown miracles, but one must still ask for rachamim.
Rabbi Tzadok learns from a Mishnah about a creature of doubtful status that a Jew shows where he belongs by fleeing to the Ribono shel Olam in a time of danger.

title.en: Fleeing to Hashem in a time of danger

summary.en: On Rabbi Tzadok HaKohen's yahrtzeit the Rav says Tachanun should be said even on a yahrtzeit, since Jews need a yeshuah, and brings Rabbi Tzadok's teaching from a Mishnah that a creature flees to where it belongs, as a Jew in danger flees to Hashem.

oneLiner.en: Speaking to bachurim at the end of Shovavim on Shabbos Shekalim, the Rav explains that guarding the holiness of the bris is the foundation that brings a bright Shabbos, true Torah, emunah and the light of the four parshiyos, and that a Jew's holy words become the shekalim offered above.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with Shabbos Shekalim falling at the close of the six weeks of Shovavim. Milah, the first mitzvah given to Avraham Avinu, is called yesod; through it one merits the Name of Hashem, as hinted in the initials and final letters of 'mi ya'aleh lanu hashamayma' and in the Name written at a bris. Bereishis hints at the sixth middah, that of Yosef HaTzaddik, which leads to Shabbos. He urges bachurim to know the relevant halachos once, briefly, ties difficulties in emunah to lack of guarding, and tells those who struggle to speak with an ehrlicher Yid and not despair. Through the wonders of animals and the lion that bowed to the Divrei Chaim he shows the power of the tzelem Elokim, with two stories. He speaks about guarding speech, teshuvah, the light of the four parshiyos, and ends with the Pri Tzaddik: the words of Parshas Shekalim become the shekalim for Michael's offerings above.

en: Milah, the first mitzvah given to Avraham Avinu, is called yesod, the foundation of Yiddishkeit, and through guarding it one merits the Name of Hashem.
The middah of the bris is the sixth middah, Friday, which leads into Shabbos; through it one merits a bright Shabbos and bright tefillos.
Difficulties in emunah and in reaching the true Torah come from lack of guarding; one who struggles should speak with an ehrlicher Yid and never fall into despair.
A person who keeps his tzelem Elokim is feared by the animals; one who blemishes the kedushas habris loses it.
Guarding the mouth is part of guarding the bris, and emunah and milah, both from Avraham Avinu, go together.
Following the Pri Tzaddik, when Jews say Parshas Shekalim with holy speech, their words become the shekalim with which the offerings are brought above.

title.en: Milah, yesod and the end of Shovavim

summary.en: The Rav opens with Shabbos Shekalim at the close of Shovavim and explains that milah, the first mitzvah, is called yesod and brings one to the Name of Hashem, as hinted in 'mi ya'aleh lanu hashamayma' and in the Name written at a bris. Bereishis hints at the sixth middah, of Yosef HaTzaddik; he urges bachurim to know the halachos briefly and says this middah brings a bright Shabbos and tefillah.

title.en: Emunah, struggle, and the tzaddik

summary.en: The Rav says difficulties in emunah come from lack of guarding the eyes, thoughts and limbs, and that our generation's tests are harder. One who struggles should speak with an ehrlicher Yid, not despair, and ask Hashem for help; only through kedushah is one sure of the true Torah. He explains why Yosef alone is called tzaddik and how yesod leads to malchus, as Friday leads to Shabbos.

title.en: The wonders of creation and how to look

summary.en: The Rav tells that the Divrei Chaim went to a zoo, and explains that seeing Hashem's creatures with the right thought brings one to awe: the lion's strength, the long-beaked birds, the giraffe's neck, the duck's webbed feet. He brings the Rambam on checking an animal's signs, and distinguishes between a glance and gazing.

title.en: The tzelem Elokim and the animals

summary.en: The lion bowed to the Divrei Chaim, which the Rav explains through the passuk that the fear of man is on all animals, and through Daniel in the lions' den: an animal does not harm one who keeps his tzelem Elokim, while blemishing the bris loses it. He tells of a tzaddik who saw an ox climbing the stairs, and the Skulener Rebbe's account of wolves that sniffed a family and left.

title.en: Guarding speech, emunah and teshuvah

summary.en: The Rav warns bachurim against improper talk, says guarding the mouth and the bris are one matter, and links emunah with milah, both from Avraham Avinu; today both are the great tests. He promises that guarding brings a happy life, and says teshuvah is always possible, as the weeks of Shovavim show, though it is far easier while one is still clean.

title.en: The four parshiyos and Michael's offerings

summary.en: The Rav says the four parshiyos correspond to the four letters of Hashem's Name and that tzaddikim felt great light in them, which one feels only when clean. He explains the shekalim that bought the communal offerings, and brings that even after the Beis HaMikdash was destroyed, the angel Michael offers korbanos above; the question is asked where the money for them comes from.

title.en: Words that become shekalim

summary.en: Bringing the Pri Tzaddik, the Rav tells the Midrash of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai, whose word filled a valley with gold coins, and explains that likewise the words of Jews reading Parshas Shekalim become shekalim above that buy the offerings. Such speech must be holy, which comes from guarding oneself; he closes with a brachah for the building of the Beis HaMikdash.

oneLiner.en: Learning Tanya chapter two with bachurim, the Rav uses the mashal of steam, water and ice to explain how all Jewish souls are one part of G-d above even though they stand on countless levels, down to the low souls of the generation before Moshiach.

abstract.en: The Rav reviews that a Jew's body and animal soul come from klipas nogah, which can be raised to holiness, while a non-Jew's come from the three impure klipos. He illustrates this with a Midrash on 'uri tzafon uvo'i teiman': the nations can bring only olos, but a Jew can bring shelamim, which are eaten, because only a Jew can eat for the sake of Heaven. Turning to Tanya chapter two, he explains that the second soul is a part of G-d above, yet souls range from Atzilus down to Asiyah, and he brings the Ba'al HaTanya's question how such levels can exist if all come from the One. His answer is a long mashal of water in a boiling kettle: invisible vapor, visible steam, water and ice are all the same water, changed on the way down. He applies this to the four worlds, the extra souls of Shabbos, warm and cold davening, the souls rooted in Adam HaRishon's head, heart, hands and heel, and our generation, the 'heel' before Moshiach, whose efforts are precious to Hashem.

en: A Jew can bring a shelamim, which is eaten, while a non-Jew can bring only an olah, because only a Jew, whose body comes from klipas nogah, can eat for the sake of Heaven.
The second soul of a Jew is a part of G-d above, yet souls stand on many levels, from Atzilus down to Asiyah.
Vapor, steam, water and ice are all the same water; the hotter it is the more spiritual and the higher it rises, the colder the more physical and the lower it falls.
So too all souls come from one root and one place, and only on the way down do some become coarser.
All souls were once part of Adam HaRishon's soul, and each draws its nature from its place in him: head, heart, hands or heel.
Our generation is the 'heel' before Moshiach, with low souls that cannot daven as earlier generations did, yet their struggle to serve Hashem is very precious to Him.

title.en: Why a non-Jew cannot bring a shelamim

summary.en: The Rav reviews that a Jew's animal soul comes from klipas nogah and a non-Jew's from the three impure klipos. He brings a Midrash on 'uri tzafon uvo'i teiman' and explains it: a non-Jew may bring only an olah, which is burned entirely, but not a shelamim, which is eaten, because only a Jew can eat for the sake of Heaven.

title.en: A part of G-d above, on many levels

summary.en: Opening Tanya chapter two, the Rav explains that the second soul is a part of G-d above, yet there are souls from Atzilus, Beriah, Yetzirah and Asiyah, as one sees in any beis medrash. He then brings the Ba'al HaTanya's question: if every soul is a part of the One G-d, how can there be levels?

title.en: The mashal of the boiling kettle

summary.en: The Rav describes water boiling in a kettle: invisible vapor at the spout, white steam rising, water falling back, and ice in the freezer. All are the same water: the hotter, the more spiritual and higher; the colder, the more physical and lower.

title.en: Four worlds and the souls from each

summary.en: The Rav applies the mashal to the worlds Atzilus, Beriah, Yetzirah and Asiyah and to the souls that come from each, from the Avos, Moshe Rabbeinu and the Ba'al Shem Tov down to the lowest souls. All come from one root and only change form on the way down; even Asiyah has nefesh, ruach and neshamah.

title.en: Extra souls of Shabbos; warm and cold Nishmas

summary.en: The Rav lists the points in the Shabbos davening where one receives the extra nefesh, ruach and neshamah. He then states the answer to the Tanya's question with the water mashal, and speaks of davening Nishmas cold like a snowball or warm like a hot glass of coffee.

title.en: Souls from Adam HaRishon's head, heart, hands and heel

summary.en: Reading the Tanya on the countless levels of souls, from the Avos and Moshe Rabbeinu to the generations of ikvesa dimeshicha, the Rav brings a Midrash that all souls were part of Adam HaRishon. Head souls are drawn to the mind, heart souls to song and poetry, hand souls to mitzvos and tzedakah, and the lowest come from the heel.

title.en: The heel before Moshiach, and davening in Karlin

summary.en: The Rav explains that our generation is the 'heel' of Moshiach and contrasts davening today with earlier generations, telling of a misnaged who davened in Karlin with Reb Aharon Karliner. He closes that the generation of the Exodus were head souls while we are heels, yet the struggle of such small souls is very precious to Hashem.

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains why dates given for Mashiach were real opportunities, brings the Ba'al HaTanya's hint of 5775 in the pasuk of the extra silver used for the vavim, and connects the missing vav of the alphabetical kapitlach of Tehillim to Yidden outside the camp whom Hashem redeems.

abstract.en: Speaking before Rosh Hashanah, the Rav notes that tzaddikim through the generations set dates for Mashiach, and asks why Ravina and Rav Ashi recorded in the Gemara a date that had already passed. He answers that every such date was truly an 'achishenah' time, ready for the geulah, but someone spoiled it; the final 'b'itah' date is fixed and unknown. He then tells how the Ba'al HaTanya, reading the Torah, read 'ha'elef' in the pasuk of the vavim as heh-elef, hinting at 5775. He asks why the vav is missing in the alphabetical kapitlach of Tehillim and replaced by a pei. His answer: the extra Yidden whose half-shekels went to the vavim, which protrude outside the Mishkan, are those outside the camp, like Bnei Dan whom Amalek attacked and the last pesukim of the Torah; Hashem does not forsake them, and 'Podeh Hashem' brings them back. He closes that our generation is at the end, and every small avodah is precious.

en: Every date the tzaddikim set for Mashiach was a real 'achishenah' time when he was ready to come, but someone spoiled it.
The final 'b'itah' date is fixed and unknown to anyone; Mashiach must come then.
The Ba'al HaTanya read 'ha'elef' in the pasuk of the vavim as heh-elef and said the geulah is hinted there in 5775.
The missing vav of the alphabetical kapitlach stands for the Yidden outside the camp, whose silver went to the vavim that protrude outside the Mishkan.
Hashem does not forsake those Yidden; with Mashiach they return, as the closing pei 'Podeh Hashem nefesh avadav' shows.
In our generation, at the end of the galus, Hashem does not expect much, and every small effort in learning and tefillah is precious to Him.

title.en: Dates for Mashiach that passed

summary.en: Before Rosh Hashanah the Rav notes that tzaddikim gave dates for Mashiach, and asks why the Gemara records a date that had already passed. He answers that each was a real 'achishenah' time spoiled by sin, while the final 'b'itah' date is unknown.

title.en: The Ba'al HaTanya's hint of 5775

summary.en: The Rav tells how the Ba'al HaTanya, reading Parshas Pekudei, read 'ha'elef' as heh-elef and would not be corrected, saying the geulah is hinted in the pasuk in 5775, and how he heard this confirmed. He asks Yidden not to spoil the year and to take on resolutions before Yom Kippur.

title.en: The missing vav in Tehillim

summary.en: The Rav shows that the alphabetical kapitlach 34 and 25 of Tehillim skip the vav and add an extra pei at the end, brings the Divrei Yechezkel that the pei replaces the vav through atbash, and asks why the vav must be missing at all.

title.en: Moshe forgets the vavim; Bnei Dan

summary.en: Returning to the pasuk, the Rav explains that Moshe forgot what he did with the extra 1,775 shekels until he was reminded that they went to the vavim, the silver hooks on the amudim, and asks why Moshe forgot. He then speaks of Bnei Dan, expelled from the camp under the Ananei HaKavod, whom Amalek attacked.

title.en: Every Yid a letter in the Torah

summary.en: The Rav explains that the 600,000 letters of the Torah correspond to the 600,000 souls of Klal Yisrael, and how the Chachamim counted them. He suggests that the Yidden outside the camp are in the last eight pesukim of the Torah, which have a different status.

title.en: The extra silver and the Yidden outside

summary.en: The Rav connects the forgetting at Moshe's passing and the last words of the Torah with the extra Yidden beyond 600,000, whose half-shekels went to the vavim that protrude outside the Mishkan's curtains. Hashem does not forsake them, and His anger at Amalek for attacking them still burns; he adds that Dovid HaMelech, in danger with Avimelech, composed the kapitel of the 22 letters.

title.en: Podeh Hashem: the vav returns

summary.en: The Rav answers his question: the vav is missing from the alphabet like the Yidden outside the camp, and the pei 'Podeh Hashem nefesh avadav' brings them back when Mashiach comes. He says our generation is the souls at the end of the Torah, and repeats that the Ba'al HaTanya's hint, also found in an earlier sefer, points to a time about 200 years after him.

title.en: Small avodah in the last generation

summary.en: The Rav says our generation needs emunah and teshuvah, brings the Arizal's words to Rav Chaim Vital that the later generations are smaller, and says that today any small, hard-won avodah is precious to Hashem. He urges using the remaining days before Yom Kippur, and closes with the hope of meeting next year in Yerushalayim.

oneLiner.en: At a lechaim, the Rav describes Parshas Ki Seitzei and the days of Elul as a time of tikkunim for souls, and then speaks of the thanks owed to Hashem for being let into Yerushalayim.

abstract.en: The Rav opens by calling Parshas Ki Seitzei a parsha full of tikkunei neshamos, corrections for souls, and mentions a tradition from earlier tzaddikim to learn the Sefer HaTikunim in Elul, a time of tikkunim. He says one should come close to such a time and let oneself be repaired. He compares this to the hilulah of a tzaddik, where saying lechaim is itself a tikkun for the tzaddik's soul, and says the parsha and the Shabbos, which draws from the parsha of its week, are tikkunim too. He mentions the Koritzer and speaks of asking for truth, and touches on the haftaros after the Three Weeks becoming a tikkun. In the second part, after wishing a good morning, he speaks of the great thanks owed to the Ribono shel Olam that, after nearly two thousand years, Jews are let into Yerushalayim, and says one must know what Yerushalayim is.

en: The Rav calls Parshas Ki Seitzei a parsha entirely filled with tikkunei neshamos.
He cites a tradition from earlier tzaddikim to learn the Sefer HaTikunim in Elul, because Elul is a time of tikkunim.
Saying lechaim at the hilulah of a tzaddik is a tikkun for the tzaddik's soul.
Each Shabbos draws from the parsha of its week, so the Shabbos of a parsha of tikkunim is itself a tikkun.
The Rav says one should thank the Ribono shel Olam greatly that, after nearly two thousand years, Jews are let into Yerushalayim.

title.en: Ki Seitzei and Elul as a time of tikkunim

summary.en: The Rav calls Parshas Ki Seitzei a parsha of tikkunei neshamos, brings the tradition of learning the Sefer HaTikunim in Elul, and explains that a lechaim at a tzaddik's hilulah, the parsha and its Shabbos are all tikkunim. He mentions the Koritzer and asking for truth.

title.en: Thanking Hashem for entering Yerushalayim

summary.en: After wishing a good morning, the Rav speaks of the great thanks owed to the Ribono shel Olam that Jews are let into Yerushalayim after nearly two thousand years, and says one must know what Yerushalayim is.

oneLiner.en: Beginning Tanya chapter three for bachurim, the Rav explains how a Jew can eat in holiness, then lays out the ten sefiros as ten powers in a person, from chochmah and binah to chesed, gevurah and tiferes.

abstract.en: The Rav reviews that every Jew has two souls. A gentile's animal soul comes from the three impure klipos, so he may only bring an olah, while a Jew's animal soul comes from klipas nogah and can be raised to holiness: he can eat for the sake of Heaven and thank Hashem even for the taste. He illustrates the higher level of tzaddikim who did not feel taste at all with a story of the Yismach Moshe and his gabbai. Turning to the G-dly soul, he explains nefesh, ruach and neshamah as service in deed, speech and thought, and opens Tanya chapter three: each is made of ten levels. To explain this he describes the ten sefiros through which Hashem created the world and the matching ten powers in man. He explains chochmah as a flash of insight and binah as building on it, chesed as love and reaching out, gevurah as holding back, and tiferes as a beautiful blend of colors. He closes with the Lubavitcher Rebbe, teshuvah before Moshiach, and a personal story of a blessing he received from him.

en: Because a Jew's animal soul comes from klipas nogah, it can be turned to holiness, so a Jew can eat for the sake of Heaven, unlike a gentile who may only bring an olah.
The Rav says one should eat calmly, with the intention to be healthy for learning and davening, and thank Hashem in thought even for the taste of the food.
Nefesh, ruach and neshamah are the powers with which a Jew serves Hashem through deed, speech and thought, and each of them contains ten levels.
Hashem created the world with ten sefiros, and man, made in the image of G-d, has ten corresponding powers: three intellectual ones and seven middos.
Chochmah is the first flash of an idea and binah is the structure a person builds on it.
Chesed is love that reaches out to another, gevurah is the opposite, holding oneself in, and tiferes is the harmony of a blend.

title.en: Eating in holiness: a Jew and a gentile

summary.en: The Rav announces the start of Tanya chapter three and reviews the two souls. A gentile's animal soul from the three impure klipos lets him bring only an olah, while a Jew can eat in holiness, with a brachah and calm, thanking Hashem in thought for the taste.

title.en: The Yismach Moshe and his gabbai

summary.en: The Rav says great tzaddikim ate only for the sake of Heaven and did not even feel the taste, and tells how the Yismach Moshe's gabbai served him every course on one plate without his noticing. He adds that this level is not ours, but everyone can eat for the sake of Heaven and thank Hashem for the taste.

title.en: Nefesh, ruach and neshamah

summary.en: The Rav explains the G-dly soul: nefesh, ruach and neshamah, received at the bris, at bar mitzvah and later through learning Gemara, serving with deed, speech and thought. He reads the opening of Tanya chapter three, that each has ten levels, and begins to explain it through the ten utterances and the ten sefiros.

title.en: The ten sefiros; chochmah and binah

summary.en: The Rav explains the word sefirah from the sapphire stone, names the ten sefiros, and says man in the image of G-d has ten matching powers, the mochin and the middos. He explains chochmah as a sudden flash of insight while learning and binah as the building a bachur makes on it into a whole pshat.

title.en: Chesed, gevurah and tiferes

summary.en: The Rav explains chesed as love that reaches out and gevurah as holding back, linking them to Avraham and Yitzchak and to the first two brachos of Shemoneh Esrei. He explains tiferes as a beautiful blend, using white and red, mixed colors and the colors of a field or a sunset, and calls it the trait of Yaakov.

title.en: The Lubavitcher Rebbe and a broken heart

summary.en: Over l'chaim the Rav speaks of the Lubavitcher Rebbe, who brought teshuvah down to the world as a drizzle before Moshiach's downpour, and tells how the Rebbe, unprompted, named the passuk 'lev nishbar' that the Rav had been saying with tears for a sick relative. The shiur ends with l'chaim and brachos.

oneLiner.en: At a lechaim in memory of Reb Shraga Feivel Mendlowitz, the Rav speaks of the Torah institutions across America that he planted and of his uncompromising truthfulness.

abstract.en: The Rav says people already felt that Reb Shraga Feivel was a special, lofty neshamah. He points to the hundreds of institutions of Torah and yiras Shamayim, chadarim and Bais Yaakov schools, throughout America, all planted by him, including Torah Umesorah, which he founded, and what he built in the yeshivah. He describes him as an ish emes who could not tolerate pretense: he did not want to be called Rabbi Mendlowitz but Mister Mendlowitz. The Rav mentions that the Ponevezher Rav spoke at his hesped, and that Reb Shraga Feivel insisted on davening slowly, asking after davening what the rush was. He then raises a difficulty on the Gemara's teaching that even if the whole world says one is a tzaddik, one should consider oneself otherwise, since the Gemara elsewhere holds that what people say is so. He closes asking that his merit protect all of Klal Yisrael.

en: Hundreds of Torah institutions, chadarim and Bais Yaakov schools across America were planted by Reb Shraga Feivel.
The Rav describes Reb Shraga Feivel as an ish emes who could not bear pretense and refused to be called 'Rabbi'.
Reb Shraga Feivel insisted on slow davening and asked after davening why people rush.
The Rav asks how the Gemara can say to disregard the whole world calling one a tzaddik, when the Gemara elsewhere treats what people say as true.

title.en: Reb Shraga Feivel: builder and ish emes

summary.en: The Rav speaks of the Torah institutions across America that Reb Shraga Feivel planted, his refusal to be called 'Rabbi', and his slow davening, then asks a question on the Gemara about the whole world calling one a tzaddik.

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains that Shemitah is Yerushalayim in time: in the seventh year the constant Shabbos of Yerushalayim spreads over all of Eretz Yisrael, and every Jew becomes like a Kohen whose portion is Hashem.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with the Ponevezher Rav greeting Eretz Yisrael with 'Gut Shabbos' on the night Shemitah began, and asks what Shemitah is. Everything exists in place, time and soul; as Yerushalayim is Shabbos in place, Shemitah is Yerushalayim in time. Yerushalayim is always Shabbos and Shemitah: nothing is planted there, it belongs to no tribe, and no one owns it, just as in Shemitah Hashem reminds the farmer that the land is His and its produce is ownerless. Yaakov, the trunk of the tree, is Shabbos, while the twelve tribes are the weekdays, the twelve Roshei Chodashim and the twelve middle brachos of Shemoneh Esrei. In Shemitah every Jew becomes like the Kohanim and Levi'im, who have no field and live from Hashem. Shemitah is not a new kedushah but an extension of Yerushalayim, like adding to Shabbos, which explains Rabbi Akiva's teaching of tosefes shevi'is. Turning to Kislev, he explains that Yishmael's bow is countered by the Jewish 'bow' of tefillah.

en: Everything exists in place, time and soul, and Shemitah is to time what Yerushalayim is to place.
In the Shemitah year Yerushalayim spreads over all of Eretz Yisrael, and the whole land becomes Shabbos.
Shemitah reminds the owner that the land belongs to Hashem; like Yerushalayim, which belongs to no tribe, its produce is ownerless.
Yaakov, the trunk of the tree, is Shabbos; the twelve tribes correspond to the twelve Roshei Chodashim and the weekday requests of Shemoneh Esrei.
In Shemitah every Jew becomes like a Kohen, without a portion of land, free for Torah.
Shemitah is not a new kedushah descending like Shabbos but an extension of Yerushalayim, a tosefes like the addition to Shabbos.
Kislev, whose mazal is the bow, is the time for the Jewish bow of tefillah to overcome the bow of Yishmael.

title.en: Shemitah as Yerushalayim in time

summary.en: The Rav tells how the Ponevezher Rav greeted Eretz Yisrael with 'Gut Shabbos' when a Shemitah year began, then explains that everything exists in place, time and soul, and that Shemitah is in time what Yerushalayim is in place.

title.en: Yerushalayim: always Shabbos, owned by no one

summary.en: He explains that Yerushalayim is a constant Shabbos and Shemitah: no planting is done there, it was not divided among the tribes, and its houses may not be rented to pilgrims. In Shemitah the land rests, Hashem reminds the farmer it is His, and its produce is ownerless.

title.en: Yaakov the trunk and the twelve tribes

summary.en: He brings the Chinuch on the purpose of Shemitah, notes that Torah goes out from Yerushalayim, and describes Klal Yisrael as a tree: Yaakov is the trunk and Shabbos, with a portion without boundaries, while the twelve tribes are the branches, the twelve Roshei Chodashim and the twelve weekday brachos of Shemoneh Esrei.

title.en: In Shemitah every Jew becomes a Kohen

summary.en: He explains that the Kohanim and Levi'im have no portion of land, belong to Yerushalayim and teach Torah, and that in Shemitah every Jew becomes like them. The sixth year prepares for Shemitah like Erev Shabbos, and in the future all Jews will be Kohanim.

title.en: Shemitah as a tosefes of Yerushalayim

summary.en: He explains that Shemitah is not a new kedushah like Shabbos but Yerushalayim spreading out, like adding time to Shabbos. With this he explains Rabbi Akiva's teaching from 'in plowing and harvest you shall rest' that one adds to Shemitah, and concludes that Shabbos has a tosefes just as Shemitah is one.

title.en: The Nesi'im, Kislev and Yishmael

summary.en: Turning to the season, he brings the Targum Yonasan that the twelve Nesi'im read on Chanukah stand against the twelve princes of Yishmael, from whom we suffer at the end of the exile. All of Kislev belongs to Chanukah, it is the time to daven about Yishmael, and the Ba'al HaTurim says that when Yishmael's princes fall Mashiach will come.

title.en: The bow of tefillah against Yishmael's bow

summary.en: He asks why the Torah tells that Yishmael became an archer, and answers with Onkelos, who renders Yaakov's 'my bow' as 'my tefillah': the bow of tefillah neutralizes Yishmael's bow, and Kislev, whose mazal is the bow, is the time for it. He mentions Yishmael's hold on Har HaBayis and closes with a call to use the time and a brachah.

oneLiner.en: Before Shabbos Zachor and Purim the Rav explains that reading Parshas Zachor weakens the inner force of Amalek, the yetzer hara, and that Purim is a day of hidden, exalted kedushah to be spent in seriousness, prayer and closeness to Hashem, not in drinking and smoking.

abstract.en: The Rav opens by explaining that everything has an inner life-force, and that Amalek's inner force is the yetzer hara that cools a Jew's emunah. Amalek cannot be fought with weapons, but reading Parshas Zachor weakens that force; it will be erased completely only with Moshiach. He asks the one reading and the listeners to have in mind to fulfill the mitzvah, links the war on Amalek to teshuvah and to coming properly to davening on Shabbos, and stresses Hodu at Minchah of Erev Shabbos. He then turns to Purim: the three days before it are like the days of preparation before Shavuos, Yom Kippur is only 'like Purim', and on Purim Hashem shows love to the lowest Jew and gives to whoever stretches out his hand. Purim's kedushah is so high that Hashem's name is hidden in the Megillah. He warns at length against getting drunk and smoking on Purim, and closes urging the bochurim to daven on time.

en: Amalek's inner force is the yetzer hara that cools emunah, and reading Parshas Zachor weakens that force even though Amalek cannot be fought physically.
Until Moshiach comes Amalek can only be weakened, as Yehoshua only weakened him; his full erasure belongs to the time of Moshiach.
The remedy for the Amalek within a person is teshuvah, and part of it is coming properly to davening on Shabbos and not talking or wandering during Hodu.
On Purim Hashem shows love to even the lowest Jew, and just as one gives to everyone who stretches out his hand, Hashem gives to whoever asks.
Purim's kedushah is higher even than Shabbos and Yom Kippur, so it is a day of serious joy with trembling, not of mockery and smoking.
Purim's kedushah comes from a level above the name Havayah, which is why Hashem's name appears in the Megillah only hidden in initial and final letters.
The Rav says that, practically, it is better not to get drunk or smoke on Purim, since many become alcoholics and smokers precisely from Purim.

title.en: Amalek's inner force and Parshas Zachor

summary.en: The Rav explains that every creature has an inner life-force, and that Amalek's is the yetzer hara that cools emunah; he cites the Gerrer Rebbe's tradition that the Germans are Amalek. Since Amalek cannot be fought with weapons, reading Parshas Zachor weakens his force, though only Moshiach will erase him completely.

title.en: Hearing Zachor, teshuvah and Shabbos davening

summary.en: The Rav asks the reader and listeners of Parshas Zachor to intend to fulfill the mitzvah and to pray for help against Amalek, names teshuvah as the answer to the Amalek that makes bochurim sin, and decries standing at the bulletin board during Hodu. He brings Rebbe Mottel Slonimer on talking during Hodu and a story of a Rebbe who put the Shabbos tisch and davening before saying all of Tehillim.

title.en: The days before Purim and its love

summary.en: The Rav brings the Vorker Rebbe that the three days before Purim are like the three days of preparation before Shavuos, and that Yom Kippur is only 'like Purim'. On Purim Hashem annulled the decree and showed love to the lowest Jew, and the giving to all who stretch out a hand, a special mitzvah beyond ordinary tzedakah, mirrors how Hashem gives to whoever asks.

title.en: Kedushas keser and the open Megillah

summary.en: The Rav explains that the kedushah of keser shines on Purim all day, more than on Shabbos, so Purim is a serious day of joy with trembling and not of cigarettes and jokes. Great kedushah is usually covered, like the shofar, the challos, the matzos and the Sefer Torah, but on Purim the whole Megillah is spread open because its kedushah spreads over the world.

title.en: Hashem's hidden name in the Megillah

summary.en: The Rav says, as something he himself does not fully understand, that Purim's kedushah comes from a level above the name Havayah, citing the Ba'al HaTanya on 'before Hashem you shall be purified'. Therefore Hashem's name is not openly in the Megillah, only in initial and final letters, and on Purim, as the King asked Esther, Hashem grants requests.

title.en: Not drinking and not smoking on Purim

summary.en: The Rav warns the bochurim not to get drunk: the true talmidim of the Ba'al Shem Tov did not get drunk on Purim, there is a machlokes Rishonim, and practically it is better not to. He describes Jews he knows who became alcoholics and smokers from Purim, explains that the habit cannot be controlled, and suggests drinking a cup of wine and lying down to sleep.

title.en: Esther and the moon; davening on time

summary.en: The Rav mentions that Esther is compared to the moon, as the Gemara says, with deep secrets in this, and recalls the Kaliver Rebbe's holy niggunim. He closes urging the bochurim to come on time to davening, especially on Shabbos Zachor and Purim, and to daven with fire.

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains to bachurim the ten sefiros, showing how the ten makkos in Egypt revealed the ten utterances of creation and illustrating each middah with examples from life and from the Avos.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with the Mishnah that the world was created with ten utterances, which come in two sets, the mind and the middos. Since no one saw creation, Hashem showed its ten powers through the ten makkos, which is why the first of the Ten Commandments speaks of the Exodus. The makkos match the utterances in reverse: the plague of the firstborn matches Bereishis, the beginning, which the Gemara counts as an utterance although it has no 'vayomer'; darkness matches 'let there be light'. He then explains chochmah, binah and daas through a student working out a Gemara, and chesed and gevurah through love and restraint, with daas as the link between mind and middos. Tiferes is a beautiful blend, seen in Yaakov, whose children were all holy, unlike Avraham's pure chesed and Yitzchak's pure gevurah. Netzach and hod are the two legs, fighting or fleeing; yesod is continuity and malchus is bittul. The shiur ends with a seudah, l'chaim and a niggun.

en: The world was created with ten utterances, which divide into two sets: the mind (mochin) and the middos.
Since no one saw creation, Hashem displayed its ten powers through the ten makkos, which correspond to the ten utterances in reverse order.
Chochmah is the first flash of an idea, binah builds it into a full structure, and daas connects the mind to the middos.
Chesed and gevurah are opposite middos, and daas is knowing when to use each.
Tiferes is a beautiful blend of chesed and gevurah, which is why only holy children came from Yaakov.
Netzach and hod are the two legs a person stands on, two opposite ways to survive: winning the fight or yielding and fleeing.
Yesod is continuation through the generations, and malchus is bittul, accepting the yoke of Heaven.

title.en: Ten utterances shown through ten makkos

summary.en: The Rav introduces the ten sefiros, explained in the Tanya, through the Mishnah that the world was created with ten utterances in two sets, mind and middos. He asks why the first commandment mentions the Exodus rather than creation, and answers that no one saw creation, while all of Israel saw the ten makkos, which revealed its ten powers.

title.en: The makkos match the utterances in reverse

summary.en: The Rav shows that the makkos correspond to the utterances backwards. Bereishis counts as the tenth utterance, the beginning before any speech existed, and matches the plague of the firstborn; 'let there be light' matches darkness, and the third utterance, the heavens, matches the locusts that came from the sky. He adds that the Bnei Yissaschar works out every pair.

title.en: Chochmah, binah, daas; chesed and gevurah

summary.en: The Rav explains chochmah as the first flash of an answer to a Gemara question, binah as building it into a full structure, and daas as connecting the mind to the middos. He defines chesed as love and giving and gevurah as restraint, and shows with the example of eating twenty cookies and of insulting a friend in anger what happens when a middah is used without daas.

title.en: Tiferes, the blend, and the Avos

summary.en: The Rav explains tiferes as a blend, like many colors in a beautiful picture, and as a rebbe's love for a talmid mixed with fear. He links the seven middos to the seven ushpizin: Avraham's pure chesed produced Yishmael, Yitzchak's pure gevurah produced Esav, while Yaakov's tiferes produced only the twelve holy shevatim.

title.en: Netzach and hod, yesod and malchus

summary.en: The Rav brings Pesach Eliyahu, printed in the siddur, that the sefiros correspond to the limbs of the body, and explains netzach and hod as the two legs a person stands on. With a mashal of a dog on a country road he shows them as opposite ways to survive, overcoming or fleeing, and ties hod to bowing at Modim; he ends briefly with yesod as continuity and malchus as bittul.

title.en: Yahrzeit seudah, l'chaim and niggun

summary.en: The Rav mentions that it is a yahrzeit that night and makes a seudah with l'chaim, blessing the bachurim with health and success in ruchniyus and gashmiyus. The recording ends with the song chassidim sang when parting from their rebbe after Yom Tov.

oneLiner.en: At a lechaim, the Rav says the nations constantly scheme against the small Jewish people, and brings the three pesukim the children told Mordechai, beginning with 'Al tira', as a source of emunah that their plans will not stand.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with a Rebbe of all of Poland whose disciples were all the great tzaddikim of Poland, among them Ger, Alexander and Vorka. He then says the Jews are a small people, the fewest of the nations, yet always make the headlines; the world constantly talks about them and everyone sets himself against them. The situation, he says, gets worse and worse, which in other words means better and better. Recalling a great war in which great miracles beyond nature were seen, he says one must rely only on the Ribono shel Olam. He retells the Midrash that when Haman sought to harm Mordechai, three children each told Mordechai a passuk, beginning with 'Al tira mipachad pisom' and 'Utzu eitzah'. With these pesukim, he says, one must strengthen oneself in emunah that the plans of the world's great ones against the Jews will not stand, and rejoice that a great time of salvation is coming.

en: The Jews are the smallest of the nations, yet the world constantly talks about them and sets itself against them.
The Rav says the situation getting worse and worse means, in other words, that it is getting better and better.
One must rely only on the Ribono shel Olam, as in a great war when open miracles beyond nature were seen.
The pesukim the children told Mordechai teach that the plans of the nations against the Jews will not stand, for Hashem is with us.

candidateTopics: Klal Yisrael as the smallest nation

title.en: Al tira: emunah against the nations' plans

summary.en: After mentioning a Rebbe whose disciples were the great tzaddikim of Poland, the Rav speaks of the world's constant preoccupation with the Jews, retells the Midrash of the three children's pesukim to Mordechai, and urges strengthening emunah that the nations' plans will not stand.

oneLiner.en: Reading the Alter Rebbe's letter 'Lehaskil HaBinah' alongside Tanya chapter 26, the Rav shows how a Jew who believes that everything comes from Hashem is not moved by suffering, and how sadness over aveiros belongs only at fixed times, never in the middle of learning, davening or business.

abstract.en: The Rav opens in Tanya chapter 26 and brings the eleventh letter of Igeres HaKodesh, 'Lehaskil HaBinah', to show what the Alter Rebbe demanded of his chassidim: to have no desire for children, life or sustenance beyond what Hashem gives, since a person is recreated from nothing at every moment and nothing bad comes from above. The Rav admits that he himself cannot live this way, and tells of a Lubavitcher mashpia who steadied himself on the way to his daughter's levayah with the letter's opening words. He explains why the letter begins with Binah: the gevuros are sweetened at their root in Binah, and he connects this with the fifty gates of Binah, Pharaoh, and Sefirah. Returning to the Tanya, he teaches that sadness over aveiros during learning, davening or business comes from the yetzer hara, and that remorse belongs at set times. He closes on how Torah brings down the light of any Yom Tov at any time.

en: In 'Lehaskil HaBinah' the Alter Rebbe asks his chassidim not to desire children, life or sustenance beyond what Hashem decides for them, since a person lives 'against his will'.
Since a person is recreated from nothing at every moment and no evil comes down from above, everything is good, only too great a light for us to grasp.
When a person truly has this emunah, the bad is sublimated and becomes good even in its visible form.
Sadness over aveiros that comes during learning, davening or business is from the yetzer hara, which wants to push a person into desires.
Remorse over aveiros is 'by appointment only': before going to sleep, on Erev Shabbos, Erev Rosh Chodesh and Erev Rosh Hashanah, followed by simchah in Hashem's forgiveness.
Torah is above time, so by learning about a Yom Tov a person draws down its light at any time of year.

candidateTopics: times for teshuvah and cheshbon hanefesh

title.en: The letter 'Lehaskil HaBinah': no desires

summary.en: The Rav picks up in Tanya chapter 26 and brings Igeres HaKodesh letter 11 to show what was demanded of chassidim two hundred years ago. He reads that a chassid should not desire children, life or sustenance, and should accept whatever life Hashem gives him.

title.en: Recreated every moment, everything is good

summary.en: The Rav explains the letter: a person is recreated from nothing every moment, nothing bad comes from above, so he should always be happy. One who feels that he lacks something loves himself and wants to leave Hashem's hand, while one with true emunah sees the bad turn into good.

title.en: Beyond our level; a mashpia at a levayah

summary.en: The Rav says he personally cannot live with such equanimity, and that he read the letter only to show what the chassidim then understood. He tells of a Lubavitcher mashpia who, walking to his daughter's levayah, shook himself with the letter's opening words 'Lehaskil HaBinah', and explains that the letter opens with Binah because the root of the chasadim is there.

title.en: Sweetening gevuros in Binah; Pharaoh and the fifty gates

summary.en: Repeating a Shabbos talk, the Rav explains that gevurah stands directly under Binah ('Ani Binah li gevurah'), so harsh judgments can be sweetened by raising them to their root. He connects this with the fifty gates of Binah at Yetzias Mitzrayim, with Pharaoh who saw blood but not that it would become the blood of milah, and with the fiftieth day of Sefirah.

title.en: Sadness during learning and business is from the yetzer

summary.en: Back in Tanya chapter 26, the Rav explains that one must serve Hashem with joy while learning or davening, and that even a businessman who suddenly feels sorrow over his aveiros in the middle of his work should know it is a trick of the yetzer hara. The yetzer wants him sad so that he will seek relief in desires such as overeating.

title.en: Remorse by appointment; the stain on the coat

summary.en: The Rav explains that remorse over aveiros belongs at fixed times named in the Tanya: before sleep, Erev Shabbos, Erev Rosh Chodesh and Erev Rosh Hashanah, after which a person should believe Hashem has forgiven him and rejoice. He gives a mashal of a stain on a coat that matters more the higher the audience, and notes that one without a program has no appointments at all.

title.en: Torah above time; the Sukkah on Shemini Atzeres

summary.en: The Rav explains that every time can hold every Yom Tov, since learning Torah, which is above time, draws down the light of Pesach, Yom Kippur or Sukkos at any time. He brings the Mishnah that one who did not eat in the sukkah the first night makes it up on Shemini Atzeres, explained in a Chassidish way as the sukkah escorting us into the house, and compares the Gemara to hidden streams that surface here and there.

oneLiner.en: The Rav asks the bochurim to strengthen the tefillah of the beis medrash in a time that calls for crying out to Hashem, and to thank Hashem every day for the privilege of being in Eretz Yisrael.

abstract.en: The Rav recalls that the beis medrash was founded on tefillah: bochurim who had davened with set seder in camp felt it missing when they returned to yeshiva and asked to continue in a shtibel. He brings the Ba'al HaTanya, citing the Arizal, that in the generation before Moshiach the main avodah is tefillah, and stresses that tefillah does not contradict Torah; one who davens with some closeness to Hashem learns differently all day. People take tefillah lightly, as the Gemara says of things that stand at the height of the world. Just as the Jews left Mitzrayim by crying out to Hashem, today, with a hard situation in Eretz Yisrael and the world, one must cry out for mercy, so he asks them to come and daven together. He then asks them to set aside a couple of minutes daily to thank Hashem for being in Eretz Yisrael, tells how Jews used to spitting on the ground had to learn to respect its holy earth, and ends with Torah, tefillah, chesed and unity.

en: The beis medrash was founded on tefillah, at the request of bochurim who missed the davening they had in camp.
In the generation before Moshiach the main avodah is tefillah, and tefillah does not contradict Torah but changes how one learns all day.
As the Jews left Mitzrayim by crying out to Hashem, so today, in a hard situation, one must cry out for mercy.
The Rav asks the bochurim to set aside a couple of minutes each day to thank Hashem for the privilege of being in Eretz Yisrael.
Being chosen to be in Eretz Yisrael when many Jews are not makes a greater obligation, to be filled through Torah, tefillah and chesed.

title.en: Strengthening the tefillah of the beis medrash

summary.en: The Rav tells how the beis medrash was founded on tefillah, brings the Ba'al HaTanya that tefillah is the avodah before Moshiach, and compares today's need to cry out to the crying out in Mitzrayim. He asks the bochurim to come and daven together, weekdays and Shabbos.

title.en: Thanking Hashem for Eretz Yisrael

summary.en: The Rav asks for a couple of minutes a day of thanks for being in Eretz Yisrael, tells of Jews from Europe who had to learn not to spit on its holy ground, and calls for Torah, tefillah, chesed and unity. He closes with a brachah to meet again in Yerushalayim, followed by singing.

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains that the whole month of Nisan is a month of emunah, shows through the gematria of the Name Havayah how matzah carries holy Names that bring emunah into a Jew, and calls on each bachur to renew himself on Pesach as all of creation is renewed.

abstract.en: Speaking at Shabbos Hachodesh, the Rav describes Nisan as a month in which the whole month is Yom Tov, a month that strengthens emunah, climaxing at the Seder, when one tells the children of yetzias Mitzrayim, the foundation of emunah. The ten plagues, matching the ten utterances of creation in reverse, testify that Hashem created the world. Everything has a soul of holy letters and Names; bread equals three times the Name Havayah, while matzah equals three times the Name with its milui. Hence 'ha lachma anya': the Names in our matzah are those eaten in Egypt. Matzah is the os of chol hamoed, so the Rav urges mehudar matzah at least at the Seder. He closes with Nisan as the season of renewal for the world and every Jew.

en: In Nisan the whole month, not only the day of Yom Tov, is holy, and the month is a time to strengthen emunah.
Yetzias Mitzrayim is the foundation of emunah, and the ten plagues testify that Hashem created the world with ten utterances.
Every thing in the world has a body and a soul, and its soul is the holy letters and Names through which it was created.
Bread equals three times the Name Havayah, while matzah equals three times the Name with its milui, so matzah is a far higher food.
Matzah is the os of a Jew on chol hamoed, so the Rav urges eating matzah baked with kedushah, at least at the Seder.
Pesach is the time when the Jewish people and all of creation are renewed, and each Jew must renew himself too.

title.en: Nisan, a month of emunah

summary.en: On Shabbos Hachodesh the Rav explains that in Nisan the whole month is Yom Tov and a time to strengthen emunah. Its climax is the Seder night, when one lowers oneself to tell the children of yetzias Mitzrayim, on which the mitzvah of emunah in Anochi rests.

title.en: The ten plagues and the ten utterances

summary.en: The Rav asks how we know the world was created, since no one was there, and answers that the ten plagues testify to it: counted from the end they match the ten utterances of creation, from makkas bechoros against 'Bereishis' to darkness against 'let there be light'. Each plague broke the klipah of heresy and brought emunah into the Jews.

title.en: The holy Names inside bread

summary.en: From 'not by bread alone does man live' the Rav explains that everything has a body and a soul, the holy letters that form it, as with 'shor' and 'even'. A Jew who washes and says the ten-word hamotzi and dips three times in salt takes in the Name Havayah three times, which is the gematria of lechem.

title.en: Lechem and matzah in gematria

summary.en: The Rav works out with the bachurim that the Name Havayah with its milui equals 45, the gematria of adam, and three times 45 is 135, the gematria of matzah. Matzah is therefore a far higher bread than lechem, and this is the 'motza pi Hashem' by which man lives.

title.en: Ha lachma anya: the same Names

summary.en: The Rav brings the question on 'ha lachma anya', how one can call our matzah the bread eaten in Egypt, and answers that the holy Names inside it are the same; the matzah is only an envelope. He then speaks of the levels of matzah, up to chaburah matzah baked by ehrliche yungeleit.

title.en: Matzah as the os of chol hamoed

summary.en: The Rav contrasts matzah baked without kedushah with chaburah matzah, then explains that a Jew needs two osos, bris milah and tefillin; on Shabbos and, according to the Mechaber, on chol hamoed the day itself and the matzah take the place of tefillin. Since matzah is the os, he urges eating mehudar matzah at least at the Seder.

title.en: Pesach, the season of renewal

summary.en: The Rav explains that at yetzias Mitzrayim the family of Yaakov became a new nation, and every Pesach the Jewish people and each Jew are renewed; this is seen below in the trees, fields and birds of Nisan and in new clothes and dishes. He calls on each bachur to become a new person in learning, davening and middos.

title.en: Brachos for Pesach, lechaim and singing

summary.en: The Rav blesses the bachurim with a kosher and joyous Pesach and with eating matzos in Yerushalayim with the korban Pesach; the gathering ends with lechaim and a niggun.

catalogTitle: בר מצוה: Sefirah Bar Mitzva ENGLISH

oneLiner.en: At a bar mitzvah during Sefirah, the Rav explains from the Zohar that a bar mitzvah is a chuppah of the soul, and that the boy, and everyone at his seudah, are preparing to receive the Torah as a 'new offering' to Hashem.

abstract.en: The Rav opens by noting that a bar mitzvah is a chassanah, which is not made during Sefirah, yet Hashem set this boy's birthday in this precious period. He reads the Zohar's account of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai's great seudah for his son Elazar's bar mitzvah, which Rabbi Yossi ben Lakunya completed by offering his daughter as a kallah. The Rav explains that a person receives nefesh at birth, ruach at bar mitzvah and neshamah at his wedding, so the bar mitzvah is a chuppah for the ruach. The boy wants to count Sefirah, which prepares a person to receive the Torah; at his bar mitzvah he gains 'ner mitzvah' and seeks 'Torah ohr', and he presents himself to Hashem as a 'mincha chadashah'. Finally the Rav teaches that every Yom Tov has its food with a neshamah inside it, and that the bar mitzvah seudah carries ner mitzvah v'Torah ohr into all who eat it, before closing with brachos.

en: A bar mitzvah is a chassanah: the boy is wed to his ruach, and so a seudah is made as at a chuppah.
A person receives nefesh at birth, ruach at bar mitzvah and neshamah at his wedding if he is worthy and learns Torah.
Sefirah is a preparation to receive the Torah, a time to purify and sanctify oneself, and its hours are very precious.
At his bar mitzvah the boy is granted 'ner mitzvah', and he also seeks 'Torah ohr', which he attains by preparing himself through Sefirah.
Every Yom Tov has its own food, and the food has a neshamah that brings the Yom Tov's gift into the person who eats it properly.
The food of the bar mitzvah seudah carries ner mitzvah v'Torah ohr, and those who eat it partake of it and are helped in their Sefirah.
