title.en: A bar mitzvah in Sefirah; the Zohar's bar mitzvah seudah

summary.en: The Rav notes that a bar mitzvah is a chassanah, not usually made in Sefirah, but Hashem set this boy's birthday now, and he cites the Avnei Nezer on how precious Sefirah's hours are. He then reads the Zohar about Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai's joyous seudah for his son Elazar's bar mitzvah, which Rabbi Yossi ben Lakunya completed with a shidduch.

title.en: Nefesh, ruach, neshamah: the bar mitzvah as a chuppah

summary.en: The Rav explains that a person receives nefesh at birth, ruach at bar mitzvah and neshamah at his wedding, so the bar mitzvah is a real chuppah for the ruach, and Rabbi Yossi's shidduch completed what was still missing. He then describes the boy's eagerness to count Sefirah, which prepares a person to purify himself and receive the Torah.

title.en: Ner mitzvah v'Torah ohr; a new offering to Hashem

summary.en: The Rav explains that at his bar mitzvah the boy gains 'ner mitzvah' and seeks 'Torah ohr', noting that the seudah of a bar mitzvah equals 'Torah ohr' in gematria. He then describes the bar mitzvah boy presenting himself to Hashem, like the one who completes Sefirah, as a 'mincha chadashah', clean and new.

title.en: The neshamah in the food; the bar mitzvah seudah

summary.en: The Rav teaches that food eaten properly feeds the neshamah, and that every Yom Tov has its food with a neshamah inside it, as matzah carries emunah. The bar mitzvah food carries ner mitzvah v'Torah ohr into everyone who eats it and prepares them for Shavuos; he closes with brachos for the boy and his family.

oneLiner.en: Speaking to yeshiva bochurim before Rosh Hashanah, the Rav shows from the number of pesukim in the parshiyos of the season that there are 122 days of teshuvah from Rosh Chodesh Elul until Zos Chanukah, warns not to waste them as in the past year, and calls on bnei Torah to learn with truth and refinement for all of Klal Yisrael.

abstract.en: The Rav tells the bochurim he will speak words of remez. The forty days from Rosh Chodesh Elul to Yom Kippur are the formation of the year, like the forty days in which the Gemara says a fetus is formed, and the Ba'al HaTurim explains zachar as brachah. He then lists the windows of judgment: thirty days for complete tzaddikim, forty for beinonim, fifty-two until Shmini Atzeres per the Zohar, and 122 until Zos Chanukah per the Arizal. Since the number of pesukim in a sedra may be darshened, as the Midrash shows with the seventy days of Haman's decree, he finds these numbers in Nitzavim, Vayeilech and Haazinu. A listener noted that Ki Savo also has 122 pesukim; the Rav explains it points back at last year's 122 days, which the year's calamities show were not used. He urges bnei Torah to carry Klal Yisrael, to learn Torah with preparation, truth and refinement, and blesses them.

en: The forty days from Rosh Chodesh Elul to Yom Kippur are the forty days in which the coming year is formed, like the formation of a fetus.
There are several windows of teshuvah: thirty days for complete tzaddikim, forty for beinonim, fifty-two until Shmini Atzeres, and 122 until the last day of Chanukah.
The number of pesukim in each sedra is part of the Torah and may be darshened.
Nitzavim has forty pesukim, and together with Vayeilech and Haazinu the count reaches 122, matching the days of teshuvah.
Ki Savo's 122 pesukim point back at last year's 122 days, which the year's calamities show were not used properly.
Bnei Torah carry the responsibility for all of Klal Yisrael, and Torah learning with truth and refinement is what protects from the birthpangs of Moshiach.

title.en: The forty days that form the year

summary.en: The Rav thanks the Rosh Yeshiva and says he will speak words of remez. He compares the forty days from Rosh Chodesh Elul to Yom Kippur to the forty days in which a fetus is formed, and brings the Ba'al HaTurim that zachar is gematria brachah.

title.en: Thirty, forty, fifty-two and 122 days

summary.en: From the Gemara, the Zohar and the Arizal the Rav lists the stages of judgment: Rosh Hashanah, Yom Kippur, Hoshana Rabbah and Shmini Atzeres, and Zos Chanukah. He counts the days from Rosh Chodesh Elul, using the Gemara's rule that a plain month is thirty days, and arrives at 122.

title.en: Counting pesukim: Haman's seventy days

summary.en: The Rav explains that the Masorah's count of pesukim in each sedra may be darshened. As an example he brings the Midrash that the seventy days from Haman's decree on Pesach until the new letters in Sivan were a reward to the nations for mourning Yaakov Avinu seventy days, and that the Megillah has seventy pesukim from the decree to its annulment.

title.en: Nitzavim, Vayeilech, Haazinu: 122 pesukim

summary.en: The Rav shows that the parshiyos read in the season of teshuvah match the windows of days: Nitzavim has forty pesukim, and through Vayeilech and Haazinu they reach 122. He then reports that a listener in America pointed out that Ki Savo also has 122 pesukim, and asks why the hint is doubled.

title.en: What the past year's events demand

summary.en: The Rav asks whether last year's tefillos succeeded, and points to the year's calamities, the earthquake and the storm in New York, as messengers of Hashem. He retells the Chafetz Chaim's derashah about the Mississippi flood, and lists the murder of a child, the passing of three gedolei Yisrael in three weeks, and other tragedies as signs that Hashem demands something.

title.en: Ki Savo as a pointing finger

summary.en: The Rav answers the double hint: Ki Savo, read so that the past year end with its curses, reminds that last year there were 122 days and asks whether they were used in Torah, tefillah and middos; Nitzavim through Haazinu give the new 122 days. He urges not to repeat the mistake.

title.en: Bnei Torah carry Klal Yisrael

summary.en: The Rav tells the bochurim that the year's destiny rests on them, as bnei Torah born into homes of Torah, to do teshuvah and take resolutions for all of Klal Yisrael. He describes the need for rachamim in Eretz Yisrael, the miracles seen there, the growth of Torah, and the state of the world that calls for geulah amid the birthpangs of Moshiach.

title.en: Learning Torah with truth and refinement

summary.en: The Rav brings the Gemara that Torah and gemilus chasadim save from the birthpangs of Moshiach, and describes how to learn: a moment of preparation before sitting down, the Maharal that the place of learning halacha is today's Beis HaMikdash, admitting the truth to a chavrusa, and refinement. He closes with the Chasam Sofer's acronym of ish and a brachah for a year of geulah.

oneLiner.en: Before Rosh Chodesh Nissan the Rav tells the bachurim that just as the whole world renews itself in Nissan, a Jew must renew himself, chiefly by strengthening his emunah through eating matzah with kavanah and through real, unhurried davening.

abstract.en: The Rav opens on Shabbos Mevorchim Nissan: Nissan is the head of the months, a time when Hashem's chesed pours onto the world and everything renews itself, from the trees to the Jewish custom of new clothes for Pesach. A Jew must renew himself too, by taking on the yoke of Heaven in Torah, tefillah, middos and chesed, and by making whole vessels to receive the blessing. Pesach is the yom tov of emunah, tied to Avraham Avinu, and matzah is an 'emunah vitamin', so it should be guarded carefully and eaten with kavanah all of Pesach. Emunah is strengthened mainly through tefillah: the Rav urges the bachurim to use the minyan of their beis medrash, to say Hodu, Shiras HaYam and Emes V'Yatziv with life, and tells of the Lubliner's notebook on the first twelve days of Nissan. He closes with Pesach as the 'mouth that speaks' and the rare Birkas HaChamah on Erev Pesach.

title.en: Nissan, the month of renewal

summary.en: On Shabbos Mevorchim the Rav explains that Nissan is the head of the months, a time when Hashem's chesed pours onto the world, when the Jews became a new nation, and when all of nature renews itself. Since everything renews itself at Pesach, a Jew must renew himself as well.

title.en: How a Jew renews himself; Pesach and emunah

summary.en: The Rav says a Jew renews himself by accepting the yoke of Heaven in Torah, tefillah, middos and chesed, and brings the Gemara about havdalah and sons to show that blessings need whole vessels. He then explains that Pesach is the yom tov of emunah, corresponding to Avraham Avinu, at whose home matzos were baked for the angels.

title.en: Matzah, the vitamin of emunah

summary.en: The Rav compares matzah to a vitamin that puts emunah into a person, which is why one is careful with the quality and kashrus of matzos and with any concern of chametz. He urges eating matzah with kavanah, especially at the Seder, and explains that eating matzah the rest of Pesach is also a mitzvah, like eating in the sukkah.

title.en: Tefillah strengthens emunah

summary.en: The Rav tells the bachurim that the chief strengthening of emunah is tefillah, and that their beis medrash holds a treasure: a minyan where one can prepare and daven properly instead of rushing. He describes how one who rushes Hodu rushes the whole davening, and explains that davening is itself emunah.

title.en: A child's kvitel and pure emunah

summary.en: The Rav explains that even a simple person praying for his own needs is showing emunah, and tells of a kvitel he once read from a young boy asking for something childish, which showed real emunah because he turned to Hashem. He concludes that one should pour out the heart in davening and say Hodu with life.

title.en: The Lubliner's notebook of Nissan

summary.en: The Rav brings from the Bnei Yissaschar that the Lubliner would write down on each of the first twelve days of Nissan what would happen in the corresponding month, and at year's end showed his talmidim that all had come true. He explains the Lubliner wished to show how each day of Nissan governs a whole month, so davening well on those days brings success.

title.en: Weekday davening, Shiras HaYam, Emes V'Yatziv

summary.en: The Rav contrasts machine-like 'factory' davening with a warm, hand-made tefillah, and notes that many daven well on Shabbos but few on weekdays. He dwells on Shiras HaYam, which brings one into emunah, and on Emes V'Yatziv, bringing the Gemara that one who does not say it has not fulfilled his obligation and a gadol's complaint that people rush it.

title.en: Pesach, the speaking mouth; Birkas HaChamah

summary.en: The Rav explains Pesach as the mouth that speaks, coming out of its exile, and says the whole month of Nissan is Yetzias Mitzrayim, an opportunity to be used. After l'chaim and brachos for a kosher and joyous Pesach, he notes the rare Birkas HaChamah on Erev Pesach this year.

oneLiner.en: Opening with a story of the Rebbe Reb Elimelech in which the forces of impurity tremble at the Elul shofar, the Rav explains that the frightening events of the time are Hashem's shofar, to be heard without fear, and calls on the people of Beitar to guard their place of tefillah and to strengthen ahavas Yisroel.

abstract.en: The Rav tells a story of the Rebbe Reb Elimelech of Lizhensk: a man captured by the chitzonim (forces of impurity) is freed through the Rebbe's letter, and he remembers only that when Elul came and the shofar was blown, they all became frightened. The Rav applies this to the present: in a time of great hester panim (Divine concealment), Hashem blows His shofar in another way, through floods, killings, the passing of three gedolim in one month and threats in the news. One must hear it and make a cheshbon, but not be afraid; he recalls how the Pnei Menachem and the Steipler kept learning during the sirens of the Gulf War. He then praises the davening in the beis medrash in Beitar, urges the people to guard and strengthen it against the Satan, to avoid disputes and to say the Rebbe Reb Elimelech's tefillah, seeing only their friends' virtues. He closes with Rachel's kosher jealousy, the need to build both Torah and tefillah, ahavas Yisroel, and brachos for the new year.

en: In the Rebbe Reb Elimelech's story the chitzonim became frightened when Elul came and the shofar was blown.
The Rav says the events of the time, in a period of great hester panim, are Hashem's shofar blown in another way.
According to the Rav one must hear the shofar and make a cheshbon, but one need not be afraid.
The Rav calls the beis medrash in Beitar a place of tefillah that must be guarded and strengthened, because the Satan dislikes it.
He urges unity and avoiding disputes, even for the sake of Heaven, and seeing only the virtues of one's friend, as the Rebbe Reb Elimelech writes in his tefillah.

He recalls the miracles after the war, the Torah's return to Eretz Yisroel, and the Pnei Menachem and Steipler learning on during the sirens, and concludes that each person must make a cheshbon in Elul.

He urges the people to guard and strengthen it against the Satan, to be united without disputes, to say the Rebbe Reb Elimelech's tefillah, and he says the signs of Moshiach are visible in the news.

title.en: Kosher jealousy, Torah and tefillah, brachos

summary.en: The Rav explains Rachel's jealousy of her sister as a kosher jealousy that begrudges nothing, brings the Gemara's dispute whether the place of Torah or of tefillah is greater and says both must be built up, cites Rabbi Akiva on loving one's fellow, and ends with brachos for a year of geulah. oneLiner.en: At a bar mitzvah, the Rav explains that the bar mitzvah day is a spiritual rebirth on which Hashem invites the boy to ask, and that Klal Yisrael's life is a circle that never ends, unlike the straight line of Amalek.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with the passuk in Tehillim chapter two, 'Hashem said to me, you are My son, today I have given birth to you,' which the Zohar says Dovid Hamelech said on his bar mitzvah day: the bar mitzvah is a new, spiritual birth. The passuk continues 'ask of Me,' and the Rav suggests this is why people give bar mitzvah gifts: our giving awakens Hashem's giving. Through a kvittel he once found at the Kosel, he teaches that requests for spiritual things are assured, since everything is in Heaven's hands except fear of Heaven. He then explains Haman's mistake about Adar: for the nations life is a line that ends, but for Klal Yisrael Adar leads into Nisan, a circle. He closes with the boy's great-grandfather, his chavrusa, whose father hosted the homeless at his Shabbos table, and blesses the boy to continue the golden chain.

en: The bar mitzvah day is a new, spiritual birth, as Dovid Hamelech said of his own bar mitzvah, 'today I have given birth to you.'
On the bar mitzvah day Hashem tells the boy to ask of Him, and the custom of giving gifts to a bar mitzvah boy awakens Hashem's own gifts.
Not every material request is granted, but one who asks Hashem for spiritual things is assured of receiving them.
For the nations life is a straight line that reaches its end, while Klal Yisrael lives in a circle in which every end leads into a new beginning.
The bar mitzvah boy is now a ring in the golden chain of his forefathers and is charged to continue it.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with the great privilege of being in Eretz Yisrael: every act there, learning Torah, washing negel vasser, even greeting a Jew, is many times greater and holier than abroad, so one must always thank Hashem. He tells how Jews from Poland, used to spitting, struggled with the habit in Eretz Yisrael, since one cannot spit on its earth. He recalls how the beis medrash grew out of loud, warm davening he introduced in camp about fifty years earlier, which the bochurim missed in yeshiva. He urges them to value the rare chance to daven at Emunas Yisrael, to come early on Shabbos and add each his spark to the flame, and to love their chavurah as the Ba'al Shem Tov's talmidim taught. He warns against speaking badly of any Jew, notes the worsening situation and the miracles in Eretz Yisrael since the war, and asks them to learn, daven and act well.

en: Every act a Jew does in Eretz Yisrael, even a simple one, is many times greater and holier than abroad, so one must constantly thank Hashem for being there.
The beis medrash grew out of warm, loud davening the Rav introduced in camp, which the bochurim missed when they returned to yeshiva.
The bochurim should use the rare opportunity to daven at Emunas Yisrael, especially coming early on Shabbos, each adding his spark to the flame.
One must love every Jew, but one's own chavurah even more, and must not speak badly of any Jew.
Though the situation is worsening, the Rav sees preparation for miracles, and asks each to do his part by learning, davening and being good.

summary.en: The Rav describes how every act in Eretz Yisrael is greater and holier, tells of Polish Jews who struggled not to spit on its earth, and recalls how the beis medrash began from the davening he introduced in camp.

title.en: Using the opportunity: davening, unity and speech

summary.en: The Rav urges the bochurim to value davening at Emunas Yisrael, come early on Shabbos, love their chavurah and avoid speaking badly of any Jew. He speaks of the hard situation and of miracles in Eretz Yisrael, and asks them to learn, daven and be good.

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains the forty-nine days of Sefirah as a climb out of forty-nine levels of impurity that Klal Yisrael also travels through in galus, and shows from the end of Maseches Sotah that the present world of chutzpah, high prices and heresy is ikvesa d'meshicha, the footsteps of Moshiach.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with the gift of the Exodus: on the first night of Pesach the Jews were lifted out of the forty-nine gates of impurity, but from the second day they had to work their own way out, refining their middos over forty-nine days until Matan Torah. Citing the Ba'al Shem Tov, he says Klal Yisrael passes the same forty-nine stages in the desert journeys and in the long galus. He shows the pattern of 42 plus 7 in the journeys, in the 42-letter Name and Ana B'koach, and in Lamnatzeach. He then explains the custom of learning a daf of Maseches Sotah each day of Sefirah: the Omer of barley is like the sotah's offering, and Shavuos brings bread of wheat. He ends that one can rely only on our Father in Heaven.

en: The Exodus lifted the Jews out of the forty-nine gates of impurity as a gift; from the second day of Pesach they had to leave them by their own work, one level each day of Sefirah.
Citing the Ba'al Shem Tov, the Rav teaches that Klal Yisrael passes the same forty-nine stages in the desert journeys and in the galus until the redemption.
Forty-two plus seven makes forty-nine: in the journeys, in the 42-letter Name said through Ana B'koach in the Sefirah count, and in Lamnatzeach.
Maseches Sotah, learned a daf a day during Sefirah, is tied to Sefirah: the Omer of barley tests the Jews like a sotah, and on Shavuos they bring wheat, human food.
The last daf of Sotah describes ikvesa d'meshicha, and the Rav shows its signs in today's world: chutzpah, rising prices and a government turned to heresy.
The Rav says a person who believes in nothing is more dangerous than an idolater, since faith, even false faith, held the nations back.

title.en: From the gift of the Exodus to the work of Sefirah

summary.en: The Rav explains that on the first night of Pesach Hashem lifted the Jews out of the forty-nine gates of impurity as a gift, and from the second day they had to leave them by their own work. Counting forty-nine days, they refine the seven middos, seven times seven, to reach Matan Torah on the fiftieth.

title.en: Forty-nine journeys in the desert and in galus

summary.en: Citing the Ba'al Shem Tov, the Rav says Klal Yisrael passes the same forty-nine stages: in the desert, a place of snakes and kelipos, and in the long galus, each era one journey. Parshas Masei lists forty-two journeys, and Rashi brings that they went back seven, making forty-nine.

title.en: The 42-letter Name, Ana B'koach and Lamnatzeach

summary.en: The Rav connects the forty-nine journeys to the 42-letter Name, which Rabbi Nechunya ben Hakanah turned into the tefilah Ana B'koach. In the siddur each day of the count carries one letter, and at the end of each week the whole line is repeated, so forty-two becomes forty-nine; the same holds for the forty-nine words of Lamnatzeach.

title.en: A daf of Sotah each day: the sotah and the Omer

summary.en: The Rav describes the custom of learning one of the forty-nine dafim of Sotah each day of Sefirah, which helps one remember the count. The deeper reason: the Jews leaving Egypt were tested like a sotah, so the Omer was of barley, animal food, like the sotah's offering, and on Shavuos they bring the two loaves of wheat, human food, hinted in the milui of Hashem's Name beside the brachah.

title.en: The last daf of Sotah: ikvesa d'meshicha and chutzpah

summary.en: Each daf brings a person closer to Har Sinai; the last day of the count, malchus shebemalchus, matches the lowest level of galus, and the last daf of Sotah speaks of ikvesa d'meshicha. The Rav notes that the Chafetz Chaim and other gedolim said it had already begun, and illustrates the foretold chutzpah with how respect for a teacher or a Rav has fallen.

title.en: Rising prices and a kingdom turned to heresy

summary.en: The Rav explains the law of supply and demand and says that before Moshiach prices rise against it, as the Baraisa foretells that wine will be dear though the vine gives fruit. He then explains that the kingdom turning to minus means believing in nothing, worse than idolatry, and tells how the Ba'al Shem Tov jumped off a wagon whose gentile driver did not cross himself before a priest.

title.en: From a world that believed to a world of minus

summary.en: The Rav contrasts the past, when kings forced their subjects to believe and Jews gave their lives rather than convert, with America, founded on belief in G-d, and with today's world that believes in nothing, which the Gemara says is worse than a house of idolatry. He brings the Baraisa about the meeting house becoming a place of immorality, and describes a Williamsburg public school built with separate entrances for boys and girls.

title.en: The Galil, the poverty of Eretz Yisrael, and our Father in Heaven

summary.en: The Rav shows the Baraisa's words on the Galil and on people wandering unpitied fulfilled in the rockets on the north and in fathers collecting for weddings, and says the whole Baraisa is fulfilled. He ends with the Gemara's last words, that one can rely only on our Father in Heaven, and urges the bachurim to be ehrliche Yidden, to daven and learn.

oneLiner.en: At a bris on Chanukah, the Rav explains that the Greeks sought to abolish Chodesh, Shabbos and Milah, the foundations of Klal Yisrael, and that milah is the precondition for learning Torah as Hashem's heavenly Torah rather than as mere wisdom.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with the Rambam's words that the mitzvah of Chanukah is very dear, explaining that what a person sacrifices for becomes dear to him, as milah was dear to Avraham Avinu because of its pain. The Greeks decreed against Chodesh, Shabbos and Milah, the foundation of Klal Yisrael: without Rosh Chodesh there are no Yamim Tovim, which is why, as the Rambam says, Eretz Yisrael was never empty of Jews, and Shabbos heads the parsha of the Moadim. The Greeks valued wisdom and would allow Torah as reasoning, but not Torah from Sinai accepted even when not understood; for that, milah is the precondition, as in the Gemara's account of the Roman emperor's nephew. He closes by saying that Eliyahu Hanavi comes in person to a bris of parents who sacrifice for Torah, and blesses the child, named Avraham Yaakov after Rav Avraham Yaakov Pam.

en: What a person sacrifices himself for becomes dear to him, and so Chanukah, won through self-sacrifice, is a very dear mitzvah, as milah was dear to Avraham Avinu.
The Greeks sought to abolish Chodesh, Shabbos and Milah, the three mitzvos that are the foundation of Klal Yisrael.
Without Rosh Chodesh there are no Yamim Tovim and no existence for Klal Yisrael, and Shabbos is the head of the Moadim.
The Greeks accepted Torah as wisdom judged by reason, but milah is the precondition for learning Torah as Hashem's heavenly Torah from Sinai.
Eliyahu Hanavi comes in person to the bris of parents who are moser nefesh for Torah.

summary.en: The Rav explains why Chanukah is a dear mitzvah, comparing it to milah for Avraham Avinu, and lists the three mitzvos the Greeks wanted to abolish. title.en: Milah as the gateway to heavenly Torah

summary.en: The Rav explains that the Greeks, lovers of wisdom, would allow Torah as reasoning but not as Hashem's Torah accepted even when not understood, which requires milah. He brings the Gemara about the Roman emperor's nephew who insisted on a bris to learn Torah, and the Greek decree that Jews write they have no portion in the G-d of Israel.

oneLiner.en: The Rav warns bachurim that leitzanus, the mocking spirit of the generation before Mashiach, uproots emunah, and through the last chapter of Malachi shows that in such a time those who fear Hashem must gather to strengthen one another.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with the Gemara's signs of ikvesa diMeshicha, the heels of Mashiach, and the chutzpah of the time. To receive from a rebbe, he says, one must stand beneath him with derech eretz, as Reb Baruch of Mezhbizh taught with the cup and the bottle. Jokes about rebbeim and teachers destroy this, and can even cost a teacher his parnassah. Leitzanus is the opposite of emunah: Pharaoh withstood the plagues only by mocking, and a single joke in a class of Reb Shraga Feivel Mendlowitz wiped out the seriousness of his talk. Emunah grows through tefillah said word by word, each word a diamond. Malachi, the last prophet, spoke to every generation until Eliyahu comes; he foresees Jews saying that serving Hashem does not pay, and promises that those who fear Hashem and gather to strengthen each other are written in a book of remembrance.

en: To receive from a rebbe one must be humble and stand beneath him, like a cup that must be lower than the bottle.
Joking about a rebbe or a teacher makes it impossible to receive from him in holiness and brings in bad middos.
Leitzanus is the opposite of emunah and uproots it, so a letz can have neither emunah nor yiras Shamayim.
Tefillah is emunah: one davens because one believes Hashem can help, and each word should be weighed like a diamond.
Malachi, as the last prophet, addressed all generations until Eliyahu Hanavi, and his last chapter speaks to the time before Mashiach.
When many say serving Hashem does not pay, those who fear Hashem gather and strengthen each other, and this is written in Hashem's book of remembrance.

He concludes that Malachi's last words, 'remember the Torah of Moshe' given at Chorev, must sustain Jews through the whole exile, even in dry times.

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains that Shavuos is a living Kabbalas haTorah each year, demanding the greatest preparation, and that its whole purpose is reached in the davening and the reading of the Ten Commandments on Shavuos morning.

abstract.en: The Rav opens by noting that no yom tov has a preparation like Shavuos: the seven weeks of sefirah and the three days of hagbalah, together with teshuvah. A Jewish yom tov is not a commemoration like the Fourth of July; the same lights of Matan Torah come down each year. He tells how the Shinover Rav saw the thunder and lightning of Sinai in Belz, and how the Kotzker answered that believing is greater than seeing. Shavuos is a Rosh Hashanah on which each Jew's portion in Torah is decided, so one must make oneself a clean vessel, as the Blazhever Rav's heart showed. The night of learning is only the preparation; like a chasan who pays for everything but buys no ring, one who sleeps through davening misses the essence. Through the stories of the Imrei Emes and Reb Yisroel of Vizhnitz, emunah, the Torah lishmah of hearing krias haTorah, and Hashem's gift of love, he closes with blessings.

en: No yom tov has a preparation like Shavuos: the seven weeks of sefirah, the three days of hagbalah, and teshuvah.
A Jewish yom tov is not a commemoration; the same lights of Matan Torah come down again each year and Hashem gives the Torah anew.
Shavuos is a Rosh Hashanah on which each Jew's portion in Torah for the year is decided.
Besides Hashem giving the Torah, a Jew must receive it, and for that he must make himself a clean vessel.
Staying up on Shavuos night is only a preparation; the essence is the davening and the Torah reading in the morning, and one who cannot do both should sleep.
Listening to krias haTorah, especially the Ten Commandments, is a way to receive emunah and to learn Torah lishmah.

title.en: The unique preparation for Shavuos

summary.en: The Rav explains that Shavuos has a preparation unlike any yom tov: sefirah, teshuvah and the three days of hagbalah. He contrasts a Jewish yom tov with the Fourth of July: it is not a commemoration, since the same lights of Matan Torah come down every year.

title.en: Hearing the thunder of Sinai

summary.en: The Rav tells how the Shinover Rav saw the thunder and lightning of Sinai during the reading of the Ten Commandments in Belz and later in Sanz, and how the Kotzker answered that his belief is greater than another's seeing. He adds that on Shavuos one is judged on how much Torah and devotion he will have, more than on Rosh Hashanah's bread and milk.

title.en: Shavuos as Rosh Hashanah; a clean vessel

summary.en: The Rav brings the Gemara that Shavuos is a Rosh Hashanah, when each Jew's portion in Torah is decided. Hashem gives the Torah, but the Jew must receive it; like costly wine that no one pours into a dirty cup, he must purify himself. He tells of the Blazhever Rav, whose heart beat irregularly before Shavuos because he had to receive the Torah.

title.en: Shavuos night and the holiness of the day

summary.en: The Rav says the success of the year, and perhaps of life, depends on Shavuos. Citing the Ohr HaChaim, he explains that on Shavuos night a purity descends because sefirah is complete, which is why one learns all night, so as to daven properly and hear the Torah reading. He describes the custom of great tzaddikim not to speak until after Mussaf, cautioning that each must act by his level.

title.en: The chasan who forgot the ring

summary.en: The Rav gives a mashal of a chasan who pays for the musicians, photographer and flowers but has no ring, so there is no kiddushin. So too one who counts sefirah and stays up all night but sleeps through the davening and the Ten Commandments: the night is only the music, the essence is the chuppah. He says one must beg Hashem in Ahavah Rabbah, and whoever cannot stay up and still daven properly should go to sleep.

title.en: Ahavah Rabbah, the Imrei Emes and Vizhnitz

summary.en: The Rav describes how chassidim once spent an hour on Ahavah Rabbah of Shavuos. He tells of the Imrei Emes, who instituted early davening and told his chassidim to sleep on Shavuos night so as to daven with fervor, and of Reb Yisroel of Vizhnitz, who told bachurim rushing to daven in order to sleep that one sleeps in order to daven, not the reverse.

title.en: Emunah, Torah lishmah and the gift of love

summary.en: The Rav explains that the Rambam counts emunah, from Anochi, as the first mitzvah, and that on Shavuos one receives it by listening to the Torah reading, which is itself Torah lishmah. He links Shavuos to the completion of sefirah and to Moshiach, gives a mashal of a lover's best gift, and closes with blessings to receive the Torah with love, awe and joy.

oneLiner.en: Facing the low days of Tamuz and Av and the trials of emunah before Moshiach, the Rav tells bachurim to ignore doubts rather than argue with them, and to truly wait and hope for Moshiach every day.

abstract.en: The Rav opens after Shavuos: the coming days of Sivan, Tamuz and Av are days of mourning, yet with Moshiach they will become the greatest yomim tovim, as the prophet Zechariah says. Until then one prepares with teshuvah, Torah, tefillah and guarding the eyes, since today's trials are unprecedented. The impurity of the street brings doubts in emunah; quoting the Or HaChaim, he says that before Moshiach Jews will fall even into the fiftieth gate, and only the power of Torah holds them. Such doubts are like a 'bug' in the head, comparable to OCD, and the advice is to ignore them and not answer, as the Vilna Gaon advised a man who saw a cross while davening. Emunah before Moshiach is like climbing a smooth wall, but Hashem is with a Jew. He describes the wars and dangers of the time, including Iran as Paras of the Midrash, and stresses the mitzvah to hope for Moshiach, who can come any day.

en: The fast days and the Three Weeks are destined to become the greatest yomim tovim when Moshiach comes, and the present days call for teshuvah together with hope.
Doubts in emunah that come from the impurity of the street are not real questions but a 'bug' in the head; the advice is to ignore them and not to answer them.
Before Moshiach, holding on to emunah is as hard as climbing a smooth wall, yet Hashem is with a Jew even in the worst situation.
It is a mitzvah to wait and hope for Moshiach; one who says 'ki lishuascha kivinu' without waiting is saying an untruth before Hashem.
Moshiach can come on any day, even before the expected time, and this year after shemittah is especially auspicious.
Every Jew carries a spark of Moshiach's soul, and each must rectify his own part.

title.en: Days of mourning that will turn to yom tov

summary.en: After Shavuos the Rav looks ahead to the fast for the massacres of Tach v'Tat in Sivan and to the Three Weeks. He says that when Moshiach comes these will be the happiest weeks of the year, describes a tzaddik who held a cup on Tisha B'Av to show how kiddush will be made then, and brings Zechariah's prophecy that the fasts will become days of joy.

title.en: Preparing for the low days amid great trials

summary.en: The Rav notes that the week after Shavuos still belongs to the yom tov, then turns to the preparation for the coming low days: learning, davening, good middos and above all guarding the eyes and thoughts. The world's impurity is unprecedented, and it leads to doubts in emunah.

title.en: Doubts in emunah: ignore, don't answer

summary.en: Bringing the Or HaChaim that before Moshiach Jews will fall into the fiftieth gate of impurity, the Rav explains why doubts are so common today. He calls them a 'bug' in the head, compares them to OCD, tells the story of the Vilna Gaon's advice to a man who saw a cross while davening, and concludes that one must ignore such thoughts and never debate them.

title.en: Emunah before Moshiach: climbing a smooth wall

summary.en: The Rav cites tzaddikim that before Moshiach emunah will be as hard as climbing a smooth wall, and Rebbe Nachman of Breslov that a Jew with simple faith then will be as great a wonder as the Ba'al Shem Tov. The Satan fights with his last strength because he knows his end is near; one must pray for clear emunah and say the Ani Maamins.

title.en: Chevlei Moshiach and the Midrash about Paras

summary.en: The Rav speaks of the wars and troubles before Moshiach, the danger to Jews in Eretz Yisroel and everywhere, and Iran's wish for a bomb. He brings the Midrash that Paras will threaten to destroy the world and Hashem will tell the Jews not to fear, for the time of their redemption has come, and identifies Paras with Iran; one must prepare with Torah and mitzvos to greet Moshiach without shame.

title.en: The mitzvah to wait for Moshiach

summary.en: The Rav brings the Gemara that a person is asked whether he hoped for the salvation, and argues that saying 'ki lishuascha kivinu kol hayom' in davening or 'ki mechakim anachnu lach' in the Shabbos kedushah without truly waiting would be a lie before Hashem. The Chachamim instituted these words for ehrliche Yidden who really wait.

title.en: Moshiach hidden in Tamuz and Av; 'hinei Elokeinu zeh'

summary.en: The Rav says Moshiach lies hidden in the months of Tamuz and Av, citing the Midrash that he is born on Tisha B'Av. Hashem asks through Tzefaniah that Jews wait for Him, and Yeshayahu's words 'hinei Elokeinu zeh kivinu lo' can be said only by one who truly hoped.

title.en: Remembering Yerushalayim; Moshiach can come any day

summary.en: The Rav brings Dovid HaMelech's oath 'im eshkacheich Yerushalayim', from which comes the custom of breaking a glass at the chuppah, and says one must constantly remember and pray for Yerushalayim. Moshiach is not tied to any time and can come any moment, even before the next Maariv.

title.en: Before its time; the spark of Moshiach in every Jew

summary.en: From the exile in Mitzrayim, foretold as four hundred years but ended after two hundred and ten, the Rav shows that redemption can come early. He points to the wars of the time and the Gemara that Moshiach comes in the year after shemittah, says every Jew has a spark of Moshiach's soul to rectify, and closes that sad days can be turned into days of joy.

oneLiner.en: At a bris the day after Parshas Balak was read, the Rav explains that the greater the kedushah, the thicker the orla that covers it, in the body, in Eretz Yisrael, in Balak who hid the spark of Mashiach, and in the Three Weeks, and that the mitzvah of milah reveals the hidden holiness.

abstract.en: The Rav opens by asking why the wicked Balak has a sedra named after him, while Nechemia, who built the second Beis Hamikdash, did not merit a sefer under his own name, because he said 'remember me for good'. He adds that the recent printing of a separate Sefer Nechemia is a message for our generation: in a time of great difficulty, a Jew must find the good in himself and take heart from his progress. Returning to Balak, he explains that Mashiach descends from Balak through Rus, so Balak's soul held a holy spark that his klipah tried to keep captive. The rule is that the greater the kedushah, the thicker the shell: the orla in the body, the wicked nations in Eretz Yisrael, and the mourning of the Three Weeks in time. Pinchas, who follows Balak, is the angel of the bris. The bris, he concludes, awakens Hashem to perform the great milah of the whole world.

en: Nechemia's sefer is not called by his name because he stressed his own accomplishment, yet today the printed Sefer Nechemia tells our generation to search out its own good points.
Balak merits a sedra because Mashiach descends from him through Rus; the name refers to the holy spark inside him, not to his shell.
The greater the kedushah, the thicker the klipah that covers it.
The pattern repeats in space, time and soul: the orla over the holiest part of the body, the worst nations over Eretz Yisrael, and the mourning of the Three Weeks over the holiest days of the year.
Pinchas, read after Balak, is the angel of the bris who removed the klipah of Zimri and revealed the holiness of Klal Yisrael.
Hashem acts like a shadow of Klal Yisrael: performing the mitzvah of milah awakens Him to remove the orla from the whole world.

title.en: Balak's sedra and Nechemia's missing sefer

summary.en: The Rav asks why Balak has a sedra named after him while Nechemia, because he said 'remember me for good', did not get a sefer under his name. He explains that the recent printing of a separate Sefer Nechemia is a message for our difficult generation: to find the good in oneself, give oneself credit and take comfort in one's progress.

title.en: The spark of Mashiach hidden in Balak

summary.en: The Rav traces Mashiach's lineage from Balak through Rus to David Hamelech, and explains that Balak tried to keep this holy spark captive inside his klipah. Through the name Ben Tzippor and the AtBash of Balak's letters, he shows that the sedra's name refers to the hidden inner Balak.

title.en: The greater the kedushah, the thicker the orla

summary.en: The Rav asks why the holiest soul was covered by Balak's hideous shell, and answers that great kedushah is always covered by a great klipah: the orla over the holiest part of the body, the worst nations over Eretz Yisrael. He then brings Pinchas, the angel of the bris who removed the klipah of Zimri, and the three dimensions of space, time and soul.

title.en: The orla over the Three Weeks

summary.en: The Rav applies the rule to time: the Three Weeks are holy days of Mashiach covered by the orla of mourning. He tells how the Plantcher Rebbe once held an empty cup on Tisha B'Av and acted out the Kiddush that will be made when Mashiach comes, and he ties the 22 days to the days from Rosh Hashanah to Simchas Torah.

title.en: This bris and the great milah of the world

summary.en: The Rav praises those present who removed the orla from themselves, and explains that Hashem acts like a shadow: the mitzvah of milah awakens Him to remove the orla from the whole world. He closes with brachos for the parents and the child and for the coming of Eliyahu and Mashiach.

oneLiner.en: Speaking to bachurim before the summer, the Rav explains how camp can be a place of kiddush Hashem: breaking one's will for Hashem, keeping away from politics and machlokes, tznius, helping friends, and coming to love Hashem by looking at the beauty of His creation.

abstract.en: The Rav opens by praising the bachurim for the kiddush Hashem they made on a recent Shabbos in Monsey, and tells them that camp too can bring either kiddush Hashem or, chas veshalom, the opposite. True mesiras nefesh, he explains, is giving up one's own will for Hashem's will, again and again. He warns against disobeying the camp staff, against arguing about rebbes and chassidus, and against politics, bringing a Rav who said that bachurim's involvement in politics is why gedolim no longer grow. From Dovid Hamelech's words in Tehillim 34 he shows that yiras Hashem means guarding one's tongue and seeking peace, not outward dress. He asks for tznius and for helping weaker friends with one's time. Then, using the Rambam, he describes coming to love Hashem by seeing creation in the country: sunsets, Barchi Nafshi, birds and animals, the story of Reb Shraga Feivel at the window, and Perek Shirah. He closes with being Hashem's shaliach and making berachos with kavanah.

en: Camp is a place where a bachur can make a great kiddush Hashem through hasmadah, davening with kavanah and guarding himself from aveiros, or, chas veshalom, the opposite.
Mesiras nefesh is not only giving up one's life; every time a Jew acts against his own will to do Hashem's will, that is mesiras nefesh and kiddush Hashem.
Bachurim should stay out of politics and arguments between chassidus'n and rebbes, and walk away when such talk begins.
Yiras Hashem, as Dovid Hamelech teaches it, is guarding one's tongue and seeking peace, not long peyos or a fine hat.
Following the Rambam, a person comes to love Hashem by contemplating His creation, which in the country is open to see while in the city it is hidden by buildings.
Hashem made the world not only practical but beautiful, so that people should enjoy it, and one must thank Him for that enjoyment.
Every food Hashem gave is both good and beautiful, so one should make berachos with kavanah and thank Him.

title.en: The Shabbos in Monsey and the camps ahead

summary.en: The Rav tells the bachurim of the kiddush Hashem they made on a Shabbos in Monsey, as a rosh yeshiva reported that they brought a new spirit, rising early to learn and davening well. He tells them that in camp too one can make a kiddush Hashem or, chas veshalom, a chillul Hashem, and that kiddush Hashem is the greatest thing.

title.en: Mesiras nefesh: giving up one's own will

summary.en: The Rav explains that mesiras nefesh means overcoming one's own will for Hashem's will, something a person can do fifty or sixty times a year, asking Hashem for the strength. A bachur who conducts himself well and is an example to others makes a great kiddush Hashem; the opposite is losing patience and treating defiance of the camp staff as heroism.

title.en: Keeping away from machlokes and politics

summary.en: The Rav warns bachurim meeting others from different chassidus'n not to argue over whose rebbe is greater, and not to get involved in the politics of Eretz Yisroel. He tells of bachurim who came to a Rav complaining about another party, and the Rav answered that in his youth bachurim stayed out of politics, and that today's involvement is why gedolei Yisroel do not grow.

title.en: Dovid Hamelech teaches what yiras Hashem is

summary.en: The Rav says that speaking against a whole community is far worse lashon hara than speaking against one Jew. He then brings Dovid Hamelech's call in Tehillim 34, 'Come, children, listen to me, I will teach you yiras Hashem', and shows from the next pesukim that yiras Hashem means guarding one's tongue and pursuing peace, not long peyos or fine clothes.

title.en: Tznius in camp and helping friends

summary.en: The Rav speaks of tznius in camp, at the swimming pool and the showers, asks for takanos there, and tells bachurim to keep away from those who do not conduct themselves with tznius because it is contagious. He then asks them to help a weaker friend, bringing the Steipler that giving away part of one's learning time to help another is tzedakah.

title.en: Coming to love Hashem through His creation

summary.en: The Rav brings the Rambam that the way to love Hashem is to contemplate His creation, and contrasts the city, where buildings hide it, with camp's fields, trees and flowers. He brings the berachah on blossoming trees, made so that people should enjoy them, and tells how he used to take his family up a hill to watch the sunset and say Barchi Nafshi, urging the bachurim to do the same after Minchah.

title.en: Why Dovid breaks out with 'Mah rabu'

summary.en: The Rav brings the tzaddikim's question why, in the middle of Barchi Nafshi, Dovid Hamelech interrupts with 'Mah rabu ma'asecha Hashem', and their answer that he was so overwhelmed by the beauty of creation that he could not hold back. He stresses that Hashem could have made the world merely practical but made it beautiful, and explains the zemer's words 'tzafra ve-ramsha' as the birds singing in the morning and the insects at night.

title.en: Reb Shraga Feivel at the window; the wisdom in creatures

summary.en: The Rav tells how his rebbe, Reb Shraga Feivel Mendlowitz, davened looking out of a window in the country, and when someone pushed him to look into the siddur he answered that he was looking in, to what the siddur's pesukim describe. He then describes the wisdom Hashem put into birds, butterflies and squirrels, and brings Perek Shirah, where a frog told Dovid Hamelech that its song is greater.

title.en: A shaliach of Hashem; berachos with kavanah

summary.en: Connecting to Parshas Shelach, the Rav says one must know he is a shaliach of Hashem sent to accomplish things. He then asks the bachurim to make berachos with kavanah, since Hashem could have fed people like a car with gasoline but gave food that is tasty and beautiful, and closes with blessings for a successful summer in learning, davening and health.
